title: Thitikul leads Open as Ryu and Kuwaki chase
description: World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.
fullText:
-7 A Thitikul (Tha); -5 S Kuwaki (Jpn), H Ryu (Kor); -4 Y Noh (US), C Boutier (Fra); -3 C Iwai (Jpn), C Wannasaen (Tha); -2 P Martin (Esp), L Coughlin (US), C Hull (Eng), R Takeda (Jpn), M Saigo (Jpn), L Woad (Eng), S Tan (Sin).

Selected others: -1 A Hewson (Eng), E Rhodes (Eng), A Fuller (Eng), L Ko (NZ), +1 M Yamashita (Jpn), +2 N Korda.

World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.

The 23-year-old has 11 top-10 finishes in majors but has never won one, and went bogey-free in a fine start to her latest attempt.

South Korea's Haeran Ryu, aiming to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year, is second alongside Japan's Shiho Kuwaki on five under.

England's Lottie Woad and Charley Hull are both on two under, while compatriot Alice Hewson led the tournament in the morning and finished one under.

"Winning one [major] doesn't mean I am going to have a really good, successful career," Thitikul said.

"Winning one doesn't mean much, I would rather be a consistent player, more than just winning one and then gone.

"Sometimes I had a hard time dealing with all the noise."

The world's best golfers performed well in the opening round, with world number one Nelly Korda one of the few stars to fall behind.

Korda remains off the pace after shooting a two-over-par 73 in a round that included four bogeys.

Korda & Hull seek major glory - Women's Open tee times

Thailand's Thitikul, who was leapfrogged by Korda as world number one when she won the Chevron Championship in April, sunk seven birdies in a faultless round.

Her round included three straight birdies on the front nine and difficult par saves.

Earlier this month, Ryu, 25, claimed her second major in the space of two weeks at the Evian Championship.

That form continued as four birdies on the front nine quickly took her to the top of the leaderboard.

Despite a bogey on the 15th, Ryu finished with two birdies in the last three holes.

Last year's Open champion Miyu Yamashita shot one-over-par, while three-time major winner Lydia Ko is even par.

Royal Lytham & St Anne's has hosted the Women's Open twice and had British winners both times - Scotland's Catriona Matthew in 2009 and England's Georgia Hall in 2018 - and the class of 2026 are aiming to keep that run going.

Woad, 22, finished tied for seventh at this year's Chevron Championship, backing up top-10 finishes at last year's Open and Evian Championship.

Having coming in as one of the favourites, her bogey-free round of 69 leaves her well poised after day one.

"Good start. No bogeys, which is always a good round here. Hit a lot of fairways and a lot of greens. Didn't make too many putts," she said.

Hull, a five-time runner up in majors, had yet another near-miss in June's US Open and will be hoping to finally get over the line.

Four birdies on the front nine gave the 30-year-old an ideal start as she aims to go one better than her runner-up finishes in 2023 and 2025.

Despite sinking six birdies, four bogeys pegged back Hull, who showed great skill to save par from the bunker on the 18th.

"I was super nervous on the first tee. I was so nervous. It's even more nerve-wracking when you're having to hit an iron because you have to stripe an iron shot," Hull said.

"I missed quite a few putts today that I felt I should have holed, but I felt like I stayed in there pretty well considering how nervous I was, because I feel there was a lot of pressure on me out there."

Hall, the most recent British female player to win a major, is back playing after giving birth five months ago.

The 30-year-old endured a tough opening round to end the day five over.

Korda started the year with two major titles, and any talk of a career Grand Slam seemed ambitious, even by her own high standards.

However, as the LPGA recognises a player as having achieved the career Grand Slam by winning four of the five major titles, Korda's victory at the US Open in June has given her a chance to enter the history books.

The 28-year-old, playing alongside Ryu, got off to a slow start with bogeys on the second and third holes but recovered those shots to reach the back nine at even par.

From hoping for a career Grand Slam, Korda will now have to fight to make Friday's cut.

title: Vic Fangio says Jihaad Campbell’s edge rusher days are over
description: The Eagles DC talks position battles, individual performances, and more in his first training camp press conference.
fullText:
The Eagles were back to work on Thursday for their second practice of training camp, and we got to hear from defensive coordinator Vic Fangio before the team took the field. He talked about some of the position battles, what he’s seen from the edge rushers, and his thoughts on individual players. He also revealed that Jihaad Campbell will no longer be getting as many reps on the outside.

Fangio said that he wouldn’t say that the starting safety spot is Marcus Epps’ job to lose, but said that the veteran has been in with the first team in the nickel group, and it’s Cooper DeJean in the base group.

“But, [Michael] Carter’s doing fine too. It’s competition.”

Fangio explained that it’s too early to tell whether Campbell will make any sort of leap heading into his second year, noting that Campbell missed the whole offseason and only had one training camp practice under his belt up to this point. Ultimately, he’s doing fine, but it’s just too early for any kind of deep analysis.

While Campbell had opportunities on the outside last year with Nakobe Dean on the roster, Fangio admitted that some of it was valuable but some was also not great. He explained that those outside reps actually set him back in developing as an inside linebacker.

The DC later said that it remains to be seen how much more they can put on Campbell’s plate, but that they were confident he’ll be able to step up. Fangio also said that the LB’s days of cross-training as an edge rusher are pretty much over, and while there might be a few times they ask him to move to the outside, it won’t be anything long term.

The DC expects Jonathan Greenard to miss most of training camp due to his pec strain, and while he’s a veteran in the league, the Eagles are asking him to do some new things — like dropping back in coverage — and those missed reps could be meaningful. Fangio thinks Greenard is capable of what they’re asking, and the edge rusher is doing a good job in meetings, but it’s not the same as practice experience.

Fangio was also asked about AJ Epenesa and how he helps fill that gap without Greenard. He explained that it remains to be seen, but also gave the DE a huge compliment (by Fangio standards).

“I told AJ [Epenesa] this — I told it to him in front of the whole team, too — for a guy that’s being asked to do a few things that he’s never done before, I thought he did a nice job yesterday with it.”

And as for whether Greenard’s injury also opens the door for Brandon Graham to return to the roster, Fangio pointed to Howie Roseman as the person who can answer that.

He later talked about how he has high expectations for Jalyx Hunt as he heads into his third year, saying that the DE is capable of being an exceptional player.

Staying healthy is the big priority for Nolan Smith this season, with Fangio saying last season was choppy for the DE because he was dealing with some injuries and missed a lot of time. Still, he’s confident in Smith, and said both Smith and Hunt had good days in their first training camp practice.

“He’s got a great work ethic, demeanor, and he just picked up yesterday where he left off last year.”

Fangio said that it’s helpful to be seeing a different offense this season, there’s a lot more moving parts which helps the Eagles defense.

The DC joked that he’s on the PP plan with Uar Bernard — lots of patience, and lots of persistence. He noted that the first day of practice in the spring was the first time Bernard ever put a helmet on, and now pads will be a whole new thing, so it’s important that he and the team temper their expectations. It’s going to be a process.

ILB Zack Baun will wear the green dot helmet and be the main signal caller this season — something he had experience doing the first half of last season when Nakobe Dean was injured. Fangio said that if they were to ever ask Baun to do something he’s not familiar with, he’ll fight through until he’s good at it, so he can do anything that’s needed.

The DC said that Howie Roseman needs to save some money to pay DT Moro Ojomo next year, because he’s someone Fangio wants in this defense.

title: UEFA’s World Cup boycott explained – and what happens next?
description: Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it? On Thursday, European football’s governing body UEFA announced that its member nations are prepared to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups. The dramatic step was a response to plans set out by FIFA, the organisation which runs global football, to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors. fullText:
Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it?

On Thursday, European football’s governing body UEFA announced that its member nations are prepared to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups.

The dramatic step was a response to plans set out by FIFA, the organisation which runs global football, to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors. The dispute could have far-reaching consequences for players, fans and the powerbrokers involved.

Our writers explain what is going on and analyse what might happen next.

On Tuesday, it was revealed that FIFA wanted to set up a new private entity — called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) — to manage the commercial operations of its showpiece events, including the World Cup. As part of the plans, FIFA announced it was looking to sell a 21 per cent minority stake in FFE to outside investors. FIFA said the company was valued at $20billion (£14.8bn) by global bank JPMorgan Chase.

Thrive Capital, the company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is expected to head up the proposed investor group.

To entice its 211 member associations, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said they would be in line to receive $40m in FIFA’s next four-year cycle if they backed his plans. He then gave them just 53 days to support the proposals — or miss out on the potential windfall.

For the plans to go through, however, FIFA needs a majority of its member associations and approval from the 37 members of the FIFA Council.

Coming just weeks after the conclusion of a World Cup dogged by controversy — including extortionate ticket prices, commercial breaks in each half dressed up as hydration breaks, President Trump intervening to overturn a red card for U.S. striker Folarin Balogun, and a surreal half-time show in the final — and following Infantino’s extraordinary Instagram meltdown, the proposals have only intensified criticism of FIFA and its boss.

As soon as the plans became public on Tuesday, UEFA issued a swift and scathing response, saying they “cross a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross”.

It went on to say how “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

UEFA and its 55 member associations later gathered for a virtual meeting on Thursday, with more than 40 associations speaking out against the proposals. They later put out an uncompromising new statement, saying no UEFA national teams would take part in any FIFA competition until the proposals were shelved.

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” it added. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

UEFA taking such a strong stance puts Infantino in a very sticky spot.

There was a call between the 41 Concacaf nations scheduled for today. In a previous statement, it said, “Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release. We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.”

The Asian confederation also said it was “disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels”.

Meanwhile the African confederation has called for its member associations to “examine” the proposals in full.

Those who spoke out in favour of FIFA’s plans included Czech FA president David Trunda — although he later performed a screeching U-turn — and Erick Thohir, the president of Indonesia’s football association, who also owns Oxford United in England’s League One, a club who have just been placed under a transfer embargo.

At the 1934 World Cup in Italy, defending champions Uruguay did not participate in protest at the low number of European teams who had travelled to the inaugural tournament they hosted four years earlier.

Uruguay again boycotted the 1938 World Cup, joining Argentina in protest after FIFA awarded the tournament to France rather than Argentina as hosts.

Meanwhile in 1966, no African nation took part in the World Cup hosted by England after they boycotted the qualifying competition in protest at FIFA allocating just one place between Africa, Asia and Oceania, compared to 10 for Europe.

Readers might think next summer seems far enough away that surely it cannot be impacted, but the European qualifying play-offs for the Women’s World Cup take place in October. If UEFA plans to boycott the World Cup, those matches surely cannot take place, as they would be attempting to qualify for a tournament in which they would not plan to compete.

Those play-offs include reigning European champions England and 2019 finalists the Netherlands, as well as Wales, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway. Thirty-two teams in total would be impacted.

And if UEFA goes along with the boycott until next summer, it would mean reigning world champions Spain and reigning European champions England — both heavily fancied to lift the trophy next summer — would not be in attendance. In fact, six of the top 10 nations would not be in Brazil.

Women’s football will be the most impacted by UEFA’s boycott in the coming months. Four of the next five FIFA competitions are in the women’s game, the first arriving as soon as September with the Women’s Under-20s World Cup, hosted by UEFA member Poland between September 5 and  September 27.

The Women’s Under-17s World Cup, starting on October 17 and ending on November 8, is set to be held in Morocco while, on the men’s side, the Under-17s World Cup follows in November and will be hosted by Qatar.

The second iteration of the Women’s Champions Cup — a FIFA competition featuring the champion clubs from each of the six continental confederations, won by Arsenal in January — is due to take place in January 2027, with the first two matches to be played in the home stadium of a team involved in each match, and the final four games to be played in Miami, Florida.

And then it’s the big one: the Women’s World Cup in Brazil next summer.

But Poland hosting the first tournament to be impacted by the boycott is certainly gripping given they are members of UEFA and would require FIFA either to find a new host entirely or cancel the tournament, given the short notice involved.

No matter how you slice it, Europe has been the dominant force in men’s World Cup history.

European nations have won a record 13 of the 23 tournaments, including six of the past eight, and have provided most of the teams in the latter stages. This summer Argentina and Morocco were the only non-European quarter-finalists, in keeping with a historical pattern that has seen UEFA sides account for 69 per cent of teams at this stage and 71 per cent of semi-finalists.

While the United States have been the most successful side in the women’s tournament, winning four of its nine editions, Europe has rapidly caught up. Three UEFA sides have reached the past two finals, with Spain beating England to win the 2023 tournament.

On the men’s side, a World Cup shorn of Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham would be a hollow shell of a tournament. Or, to put it in terms FIFA’s proposed investors might better understand, it would strip the competition of its most valuable assets.

German website Transfermarkt provides estimates of players’ values, and each of its 10 most valuable players hails from a European nation. Of the 104 players valued at €50million (£42.8m; $57.6m) or more, 77 play for UEFA sides. FIFA’s proposal aims to maximise the tournament’s commercial appeal, but without these star talents, the value of the enterprise would collapse.

Similarly, the women’s event would be lacking some truly stellar names. Aitana Bonmati, who has won the last three Ballons d’Or, would be absent, as would her Spain compatriot Alexia Putellas. England’s Leah Williamson, Lauren James and Alessia Russo, too.

In fact, the entire top 10 of last year’s Ballon d’Or Feminin (Bonmati, Mariona Caldentey, Russo, Putellas, Chloe Kelly, Patri Guijarro, Williamson, Ewa Pajor, Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton) would be unavailable for the tournament, not to mention exciting young talent in Norway’s Signe Gaupset or France’s Alice Sombath.

It would mean a World Cup without the world’s best, which is hardly what a World Cup should be.

Conor O’Neill and Megan Feringa

Damaging? This destroys it. There is no FIFA Forward Enterprise without European nations taking part in its competitions.

Critics of Infantino’s plan were heartened by the initial negative response it received from the confederations in Asia, Europe and North and Central America, but were worried that the tone of those responses was more “why is this the first we are hearing of this idea”, as opposed to “this is a dreadful idea, just stop”.

And those concerns about the strength of the opposition to Infantino grew when the likes of the English, French and German federations all put out statements that were more focused on the process than the principle.

They need not have worried, though. Because we now know that UEFA and its member associations were just taking a few moments to find their backbones and clear their throats.

This is another European Super League moment. European football has correctly realised that this idea cannot be allowed to gain momentum. If Infantino could have dragged this through to his September 19 deadline, it would have been too late to stop it. He would have had two thirds of the planet, at least, on board. So, Europe has gone nuclear. We will not come to play. And without us, what have you really got to sell?

If this outbreak of unity lasts the weekend, FFE is OFF.

A lot. FIFA is keen to talk up taking football to the world, and equally keen to keep expanding its showpiece, but it remains the case that European nations provide the bulk of the tournament’s quality and, thus, the World Cup’s appeal.

Six of this year’s eight quarter-finalists were UEFA nations, and since money is apparently the main thing football’s governing body pays attention to these days, a quick look at who took home the most in performance-based payments from the World Cup quite neatly highlights how crucial UEFA teams are to FIFA’s pièce de résistance.

After stripping out the $10million all 48 teams got for showing up this summer, and $2.5m in preparation fees, FIFA doled out $223m on a performance basis. UEFA’s 16 teams hoovered up $127m of that. Put another way: one-third of the teams took home nearly two-thirds of the performance-based payments.

A World Cup without those teams would be dramatically diminished.

It absolutely should, right? You cannot with one breath say you are not going to play in the next World Cup but then, in the next, say, “We would still like to host one, though”.

No, if this boycott is to mean anything, it has to be a total boycott. FIFA, its sponsors and broadcasters, and its potential investors, need to know that Europe is off the table if Infantino presses on with FFE.

The funny thing is, some in the game thought it was incredibly unhelpful to UEFA’s cause that the German FA gave an interview to, ahem, The Athletic about its wish to host the 2038 or 2042 men’s tournament the day before Infantino announced this plan.

But then, in the German FA’s defence, it clearly did not know what Infantino had been plotting. After all, its boss only sits on the FIFA Council and those guys are the last people Infantino speaks to about his plans.

Yeah, sure, but only if the rebel alliance starts to fracture.

Europe may only have 55 of the 211 votes at FIFA but it has a far, far bigger share of FIFA’s commercial value because its nations have been providing the lion’s share of the teams, players and winners of FIFA’s competitions forever. Only South America has come close to Europe’s outsized impact and influence.

If Europe stays united on this, Europe wins this row. If some of UEFA’s members start to think they might like $40million to pay off their debts, build their own St George’s Park or hire Pep Guardiola, then Infantino can turn this around.

But everything we are hearing suggests European football really means it. They don’t like the process or the principle. And that mirrors what most European football fans think, too.

Might this view upset those parts of the world that really liked this idea? Those parts of the world that look at the European game with envy and frustration? Those parts of the world that find Europeans a bit preachy and selfish?

Yes, yes and yes. But that does not mean Europe is wrong in this regard. Putting any philosophical objections to “selling the World Cup” to one side, this is not a very good deal for global football. If it wants to go down this road, it could do a lot better.

Some in Europe will also point out that the rest of global football will continue to think Europe needs taking down a peg or two regardless of whether this deal goes through or not, so Europe might as well take the brickbats and be right.

In almost any other business or walk of life, this would be a resignation matter. But Infantino deciding to fall on his sword would arguably be even more surprising than his attempt to sell a fifth of FIFA’s revenues to a group of investors led by Ivanka Trump’s brother-in-law.

Prior to this week’s Infantino brainwave, there seemed little to no chance that anyone would stand against him when the next election for a FIFA president takes place in Morocco in March.

That is not to say everyone loves him — they do not — but nobody believed anyone else would stand a chance in that election, so what was the point?

Is that still the case now? Let us see how he responds to UEFA’s surprisingly strident rejection of this idea.

If he shrugs and says, “OK, I’ve heard you, we won’t do it — it was just a consultation exercise, anyway”, he very probably survives. He has done this type of thing a few times before and bounced back every time, usually with a new idea.

It is entirely possible, for example, that he quickly admits defeat on this one but then quickly comes back and says, “Right, Europe, you didn’t like that idea but FIFA has got to even the playing-field somehow, so let’s have 64-team World Cups with more money and slots for Africa and Asia”. That would be very on brand.

But if he ploughs on with FFE, hoping that UEFA starts to crumble… well, it becomes a case of last-man standing: him or Aleksander Ceferin, and Ceferin has the better weapons at the moment.

That does not mean that Ceferin would be the most likely successor to Infantino, though. For the reasons outlined above, he is not that popular outside Europe and he has not hidden his disdain for FIFA politics very well.

This is why seasoned FIFA watchers believe Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari boss of beIN Media and the president of European Football Clubs, is a far better shout as he spans Asia and Europe, as well as big clubs and media partners.

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

title: Mets Reportedly Not Discussing Extension With Coveted Trade Candidate
description: The New York Mets could look to trade Clay Holmes this week
fullText:
The New York Mets are expected to be one of the most active sellers this week, leading up to the MLB trade deadline.

Among the players who could be dealt is pitcher Clay Holmes. After spending years as an All-Star reliever for the New York Yankees, Holmes signed a three-year, $38 million deal with the Mets as a starter. He had a solid first season as a starter, posting a 3.53 ERA.

This year, he had a 2.39 ERA through nine starts. Unfortunately, he fractured his fibula after taking a comebacker off the leg. He is currently on a rehab assignment, and during his last rehab start, scouts from the New York Yankees, Chicago White Sox, Philadelphia Phillies, Tampa Bay Rays, Rangers, Los Angeles Dodgers and Arizona Diamondbacks were present.

Teams are interested in him for sure. He has a $12 million player option for next season that he is likely to decline after establishing himself as a valuable starter. The Mets could try to keep him around after two strong seasons, but apparently they are not interested in that.

Looking for the perfect gift for a baseball player in your life? Check out our brand new baseball lifestyle brand!

"There’s no extension talk ongoing with Mets starter Clay Holmes, so presumably there will be no extension," wrote MLB insider Jon Heyman on X on Thursday. "In this sellers market, with precious few frontline starters available, this is a big trade piece. Nearly every contender scouted him in rehab game."

Holmes has looked good in his rehab appearances and could play very well on a team with an elite defensive infield. He gets a ton of ground balls and could be very successful on a team like the Milwaukee Brewers or Atlanta Braves.

title: VOLLEYBALL: Balanced attack powers Claremore to 5 team-camp wins
description: No matter which lineup took the floor Tuesday, Claremore found a way to win. That was exactly the kind of problem coach Derek Jackson wanted to have. The Lady Zebras put their depth on full display during Tuesday's team camp at the Doug K. Mosier Athletic Complex, posting victories over Sand Springs, Glenpool, Sapulpa, Collinsville and Ponca City while experimenting with multiple lineups ahead ...
fullText:
No matter which lineup took the floor Tuesday, Claremore found a way to win.

That was exactly the kind of problem coach Derek Jackson wanted to have.

The Lady Zebras put their depth on full display during Tuesday's team camp at the Doug K. Mosier Athletic Complex, posting victories over Sand Springs, Glenpool, Sapulpa, Collinsville and Ponca City while experimenting with multiple lineups ahead of the 2026 season.

Claremore received production from throughout the roster, led by senior middle Addison Doyle, who dominated at the net with 22 kills, 9 blocks and 9 aces.

Outside hitter Ava Tanner added 19 kills, 18 digs and 2 blocks, while Emme Baker contributed 15 kills and 3 aces. Bella Hoisington also controlled the front row with 12 kills and 6 blocks.

Setter Grace Baughman filled the stat sheet with 6 kills, 7 aces, 35 assists, 25 digs and 5 blocks, while fellow setter Maise Stagner-Speer dished out 36 assists to go with 4 aces and 3 kills.

Defensively, Madison Godding anchored the back row with 35 digs while adding 11 assists and 4 aces. Mariyah Dupuch chipped in 12 digs and an ace, while sophomore Ivorie Baker sparked the Lady Zebras with 7 aces and 6 kills.

Madison Berger, Audrey Shaw and Alexis Freeman rounded out the balanced attack with a combined 13 kills.

Following the dominant performance, Jackson said the day reinforced just how much versatility his team possesses entering the final stretch of preseason preparation.

"Really good day of volleyball for us," Jackson said. "We tried all sorts of lineups and combinations, and in all of them we showed some really good stuff. Our seniors are all doing a great job. Mix in those talented underclassmen, and we have lots of options and depth going into the season."

Jackson added that the team's recent practices have helped solidify roles as the Lady Zebras inch closer to opening day.

With five victories Tuesday and continued competition still ahead, Claremore appears to be building momentum as it prepares to open the regular season.

"These couple of weeks of practice are really starting to iron out some things, and we are going to be starting the season at a very high point," he said. "We still have a full week of practices and our annual super scrimmage to continue helping us grow.

"Opening Day will be a big tell of just how good this team can be."

title: Indiana's Curt Cignetti: The Big Ten is the best conference because 'we don't cry a river, whine, and complain' after falling short
description: Big Ten teams have won the last three national championships and the conference is well-positioned for four straight titles.
fullText:
There's no doubt that Curt Cignetti believes the Big Ten is the best conference in college football heading into the 2026 season.

Cignetti's Hoosiers are looking to become just the second team in the playoff era to win back-to-back national championships in 2026. As Indiana went 16-0 and won the national title in January, it was the third straight Big Ten team to win the College Football Playoff.

Georgia, which went back-to-back in 2021 and 2022, is the last SEC team to win a title. And while Cignetti thought it was a "loaded question" at Big Ten media days on Thursday when asked whether the Big Ten's nine-game conference schedule was a positive or a negative for the playoff, he used that question as an opportunity to tout the conference's strength.

And also potentially make an indirect dig at another.

"I think that's a loaded question. I think your job as a head coach and the assistants, is to equip your roster, make it as strong as possible with adequate depth at every position throughout the team," Cignetti said. "When you play that many games you're going to get some guys dinged and injured, things happen. Next man up mentality.

"The Big Ten is the best league in football and a lot of really good football teams. It's hard to win on the road. Very physical football teams. Very well-coached. It definitely prepares you for the playoffs, there's no doubt about it, the numbers speak for themselves.

"We don't run a hype machine up here in the Midwest, we believe that everything's earned, not given. And when we fall short we say we fell short. We don't cry a river, whine, and complain. Alright? And that's why we're the best."

You can certainly quibble with the statement that the Big Ten doesn't run a hype machine. The conference is very proud of its three straight national titles and has a really good chance at a fourth consecutive one. Indiana, Oregon and Ohio State all enter the season as legitimate national title contenders and are among the top five betting favorites to win the national title.

Texas, the No. 2 favorite behind Ohio State, is the only SEC team in the top five.

The SEC's only claim to being the best conference is with its depth. You can make the strong case that the SEC is the deepest conference in college football. But while the SEC had five teams in the playoff a season ago, the Big Ten had three. And all there of the Big Ten's teams were among the top five seeds.

Indiana doesn't have a cakewalk to a third straight CFP appearance either. After playing two ranked teams during the regular season in 2025 thanks to Penn State's demise, the Hoosiers have games against Ohio State, Michigan, USC and Washington all in the second half of the season. If USC is as good as coach Lincoln Riley says it is, the Big Ten could be even better in 2026. And Cignetti's words could turn out to be hardly be controversial in SEC country.

title: England's Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer
description: England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.
fullText:
England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.

The 32-year-old left City when his contract expired at the end of last month, while playing for England at the World Cup where he helped them to a third-placed finish.

Stones has signed a two-year deal with Inter, a club statement said.

He played five times for England at the recent World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada, making his 94th international appearance in the semi-final loss to Argentina.

Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.

His final few seasons at the Etihad Stadium, though, were hit by injuries, and he only made nine Premier League appearances last term.

Stones could make his Inter debut when they start their Scudetto defence against Monza at the San Siro on August 22.

title: Mendoza-mania and the defensive search for identity early storylines for Raiders
description: Before training camp began, Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak established the pecking order at quarterback.
fullText:
Before training camp began, Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak established the pecking order at quarterback.

Kirk Cousins would be the one starting things off atop the depth chart, while Fernando Mendoza would be tasked with challenging him. The decision was twofold: turn to the veteran Cousins to provide some stability as the Raiders continue to work their way through Kubiak’s offense, while ensuring the rookie Mendoza receives the proper development and is not rushed into the lineup too soon.

It was a message that Mendoza took to heart, and one that has been doing its job to motivate the first overall pick to improve every day as training camp rolls on.

“I was telling some of the other quarterbacks this: when it was rookie minicamps and OTAs, they happen very quick. However, now in training camp, I feel like a member of the team rather than a new rookie on the scene,” said Mendoza describing his efforts after two days of training camp.

“Every day, it’s more and more reps that I get. I feel like the entire team improves…every single rep we get, so the more experience out there on the field, the more beneficial for everybody.”

While Cousins put together a strong day in his own right, Mendoza was equally impressive with some of the throws he put together. From throws requiring pinpoint precision to the likes of Jack Bech and Brandon Johnson, to perfectly placing a ball downfield to Deven Thompkins, Mendoza impressed not only with his accuracy, but willingness to read the field and make the correct play over the flashy one.

It was not a perfect day from the rookie; a pair of throws towards the end of the team period were off on the timing by just a hair. However, it did little to dampen Mendoza’s seemingly boundless enthusiasm, as he has gotten used to correcting himself and learning over his first few months as a Raider.

“I think it also stems from the relationship everyone had with each other, especially if you’ve seen OTAs and Day One, and even today on Day Two…there’s a lot of times where the offensive line would correct me,” admitted Mendoza. “The running backs, the tight ends, the receivers, they would help put me in place, so it’s our relationship that we have. That dynamic relationship where we are able to hold each other accountable, but not in a way of being demeaning or in a negative light, but in a positive.”

While the offense continues to impress early on, it also showcases a defense still looking to solidify an identity under first-year defensive coordinator Rob Leonard.

New faces such as Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker are still getting acclimated to their teammates, while other positions are still up for grabs. For example, Eric Stokes and Taron Johnson seem to have good grasps on two of the three cornerback spots, but the outside spot opposite Stokes is still up for grabs. Rookie Hezekiah Masses and Darien Porter have been splitting first-team reps early, and it remains to be seen if Jermod McCoy will factor into the equation at some point.

“It truly is competitive, from the ones, the twos, the threes,” said Leonard about the competition, with an emphasis on how quickly Masses has come in such a short amount of time. “We’re really trying to make it a fair competition, but he’s controlling everything he can. He’s that good balance right now of being humble as a rookie, but being confident enough and what we’re asking him to do to go out and execute.”

While the defense would get gashed both through the air and on the ground in the early going, they seemed to pick up some ground later on. Maxx Crosby would get the edge on Kolton Miller on a rep to get pressure against Cousins, McCoy would get a pass breakup and Dean was fingertips away from a diving interception after a drop. The defense would also end the day strong with a forced fumble during a situational drill.

“They can do it and then we track it, like how much ball production we have today,” said Leonard about his defense having the ball skills to force turnovers. “I go back to the red blinking meter: if we didn’t have any PBUs, batted balls, interceptions, what do we got to do to fix it?”

It is unsurprising that the early days of training camp would feature growing pains as well as highlights, due to the new systems and culture being implemented all at once. However, what matters most is getting an early identity down and sticking with it, creating a foundation the Raiders can build on through the beginning of the season.

“I think we’re going to be the most conditioned team, the most physical team and we’re going to play together,” running back Ashton Jeanty said when asked about his early impressions of the Raiders’ identity.

The name of the game for the Raiders this season is improvement, and every player is willing to step up one day at a time to make it happen.

title: Rockies' asking price for Hunter Goodman could be too much for the Red Sox
description: As the Red Sox search for a trade deadline blockbuster, another target may just have too high a price.
fullText:
Rockies' asking price for Hunter Goodman could be too much for the Red Sox originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

With only a few days till the trade deadline, the Boston Red Sox need to make a big move, especially with the fact that newly acquired second baseman Curtis Mead is going to be out for 6-8 weeks with a fractured wrist.

One of Boston’s top priorities is getting another slugger, preferably right-handed and either a catcher or shortstop. For catchers, Colorado Rockies two-time All-Star Hunter Goodman is the best option on the market, as he is one of the best sluggers in the game this season. However, his asking price might make Boston balk.

According to The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal, the Rockies want a large package headlined by the best prospect in the suitor’s farm, name-dropping the Red Sox and their No. 1, Franklin Arias.

“The Rockies, however, face no urgency to move Goodman, who is under club control for three additional seasons. So, they’re asking for multi-player packages led by teams’ No. 1 prospects — outfielder Theo Gillen from the Rays, Franklin Arias from the Red Sox and so on,” Rosenthal wrote.

So, some combination of Arias, and some other young players with control, such as Marcelo Mayer, and probably Carlos Narvaez to replace Goodman as a catcher is what Colorado wants from Boston.

WooSox Photo/Ashley Green / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images

Arias is currently the No. 7 prospect in the Top 100, and was recently promoted to AAA Worcester after slashing .318/.407/.587/.993 with 17 doubles, 19 home runs, and 52 RBI in 75 games at AA.

There’s even a chance that Arias could be a late-September call up for the Red Sox, so dealing him may be out of the question. However, with a possible 2027 lockout looming, Boston could be looking to go all-in this season on a playoff run.

Honestly, even with the three years of team control, if Boston wants to deal their No. 1 prospect, it should be for something with a bigger return.

ESPN’s Jeff Passan noted that there is a potentially bigger trade out there for Boston, where they could kill two birds with one stone: getting both their catcher and shortstop that they wanted from the Miami Marlins in Otto Lopez and Liam Hicks. In a deal like that, it makes more sense to deal Arias, or find a way to keep him but give up more for the deal.

Hopefully, Boston has their plans set in motion, as their time is running out.

fullText:
The Sequoyah Classic is next month, and the Lady Eagles are hoping the community can help make sure visitors leave with more than just great matches.

Sequoyah volleyball is seeking baked goods and treat donations for its annual bake sale during the Sequoyah Classic Tournament, scheduled for Friday, Aug. 14, and Saturday, Aug. 15.

All proceeds from the fundraiser will go directly toward the program's goal of purchasing a portable net system for the Lady Eagles.

The program is asking community members to donate homemade or store-bought treats, including cookies, brownies, cakes, breads and other baked goods. Individually wrapped items are especially encouraged because they are ideal for single-serving sales during the tournament.

Organizers prefer donations be dropped off by Thursday, Aug. 13, though baked goods will also be accepted on the morning of Friday, Aug. 14, before tournament play begins.

Those interested in contributing are asked to comment on the team's social media post or send the program a direct message to coordinate their donation.

In addition to raising money for new equipment, the bake sale gives the Lady Eagles an opportunity to welcome teams and fans from across the region while showcasing what the program calls "Eagle hospitality."

With dozens of players, coaches and spectators expected to attend the two-day tournament, Sequoyah hopes community support will help make the fundraiser and the tournament a success.

title: Liverpool dealt knockout blow in pursuit of talented forward
description: Liverpool Transfer News: Rayan Interest Faces Fresh Doubt After Bournemouth Injury BlowLiverpool’s search for attacking reinforcements has largely centred on Paris Saint-Germain forward Bradley Barc...
fullText:
Liverpool’s search for attacking reinforcements has largely centred on Paris Saint-Germain forward Bradley Barcola in recent weeks, but another name has consistently surfaced in discussions, AFC Bournemouth winger Rayan.

During the latest edition of Media Matters on Anfield Index, Dave Davis and David Lynch explored whether Liverpool’s long standing admiration for the Brazilian could realistically develop into a move this summer. Their conclusion was clear. Bournemouth’s circumstances, particularly following Junior Kroupi’s serious injury, make any deal appear increasingly unlikely.

The discussion began after Dave Davis highlighted fresh reports surrounding Bournemouth’s squad.

Referencing David Ornstein’s update, Davis noted that Junior Kroupi had suffered a foot injury in training that would require surgery and leave the forward sidelined for three to four months.

“I mean, that probably ends anything you think of Rayan coming in the short term,” Davis suggested. “It’s just hard to see now Kroupi’s got that injury.”

Lynch agreed that Bournemouth’s situation had become significantly more complicated.

“I think so. I just think the fee would be too much as well, obviously, as the release clause doesn’t kick in until next summer.”

That assessment points towards two major obstacles, Bournemouth’s strengthened negotiating position and Liverpool’s reluctance to pay well above the future release clause.

Rather than viewing this summer as the ideal opportunity, Lynch suggested Liverpool may actually benefit from delaying any move.

“The kind of money they’d be asking, I still think Liverpool would probably want a little bit more evidence of what he can do in the Premier League as well.”

He explained why next summer could present a much cleaner opportunity.

“The fact that the release clause comes in in 2027, I think it kind of works for everyone really, Liverpool get a bit of a closer look and an idea of just how good he is at that point. And then that release clause is sat there.”

Rather than rushing into an expensive transfer, Liverpool would gain another full Premier League season to evaluate the Bournemouth attacker.

Although Rayan has regularly been linked with Liverpool, Lynch admitted he had never believed a move was particularly realistic during this window.

“For me, I’ve never really bought into that, that was one that was possible, to be honest.”

He also pointed towards Liverpool’s own emerging talent as another factor that could influence future recruitment.

“In 2027, you also get a clearer idea of where Abe was up to, where Ngumoha is in his development as well.”

With several academy prospects continuing to impress under Andoni Iraola, Liverpool may have greater clarity before committing significant funds to another young winger.

Throughout the podcast, Bradley Barcola remained the dominant transfer topic, with Lynch repeatedly expressing confidence that Liverpool’s negotiations with Paris Saint-Germain are moving in the right direction.

Against that backdrop, Rayan appears to have slipped further down Liverpool’s list of immediate priorities.

Lynch concluded that Bournemouth’s latest injury setback only strengthens their determination to retain one of their brightest attacking talents.

“I think with Bournemouth having an injury there to Kroupi, they’re going to be even more kind of resolved to not let any big stars go.”

For Liverpool, patience may ultimately prove the smarter strategy. Rayan remains a player they admire, but the combination of Bournemouth’s asking price, the delayed release clause and Kroupi’s lengthy absence means this increasingly looks like a transfer for another window rather than this summer.

title: ‘Football is not for sale’: Uefa confirms boycott of World Cup and Fifa competitions
description: ‘No Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition’ while Gianni Infantino’s plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup remain alive, says the organisation
fullText:
Football’s European governing body has announced a full boycott of Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its tournaments to private investors are voted through.

The drastic action, which follows an emergency meeting on Thursday, was “unanimously” agreed among all 55 of Uefa’s member associations. A statement confirmed that “no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive”.

World Cup boycott latest: Uefa agree emergency action after Infantino sell-off plan

Uefa carries significant leverage as a World Cup without major nations such as champions Spain, France, England and Germany would compromise Infantino’s designs on extracting as much revenue from the global showpiece as possible. Six of the eight quarter-finalists from this summer’s World Cup were European.

It would also harm next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, with Spain the reigning winners and European champions England also bringing considerable commercial interest in the tournament. England, runners-up at the 2023 World Cup, face two-legged qualification play-offs in October, as do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

A spokeswoman for the English FA echoed the Uefa sentiment, saying: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Meanwhile, the majority of the 2030 World Cup will be staged in Europe, with Spain and Portugal sharing hosting rights along with Morocco, following games in South America hosted by Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay to commemorate the tournament’s centenary year.

On Tuesday, Fifa revealed plans to create a new $20bn subsidiary, 20 per cent owned by private investors, to manage the commercial rights and delivery of the World Cup and other major tournaments. Thrive Eternal, led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is set to lead the new investment.

“This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football,” Uefa said. “The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure.”

In a letter to the member associations, Infantino promised that national federations would benefit from an increase of its “Fifa Forward” funding from around $8m to $20m for the upcoming four-year cycle between 2027 and 2031 if the new FFE subsidiary is created.

Additionally, the letter states that a “one-off” payment of another $20m would be made available for member associations who vote for Infantino’s proposals on 19 September. Member associations are then warned that their funding for the 2027-2031 cycle would only stand at $10m if the vote does not pass, meaning they would miss out on $30m.

Uefa’s statement added: “National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”

Many of the world’s smaller countries, especially those outside of Europe, are more dependent on funding from Fifa to run their national teams, develop long-term grassroots projects and invest in infrastructure, like pitches, academies and stadiums. Before this year’s World Cup, Infantino claimed that “without Fifa, there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”.

Uefa’s confirmation that it would stage a boycott comes ahead of a vote between Fifa’s 211 member associations on 19 September. Infantino’s proposals only require a majority vote of above 50 per cent, as well as backing from the Fifa Council, which means Uefa still requires more support from another federation, such as North America or Asia, to have a chance at winning the vote and avoiding a boycott.

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

“It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

“But our opposition goes far beyond process.

“The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

“This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

“Europe’s position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

“Nobody should be in any doubt: Uefa and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

“There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

“Some things are simply too important to sell. The Fifa World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

title: McAllister accuses FIFA of 'blackmail' over World Cup plan
description: Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister has accused Fifa of trying to blackmail member associations into trying to accept its controversial private equity plan.
fullText:
Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister has accused Fifa of trying to blackmail member associations into trying to accept its controversial private equity plan.

European football's governing body has made a definitive stance against the Fifa proposals to sell stakes in major competitions.

The position was backed up when Uefa's 55 member associations voted to boycott the World Cup in response.

That was despite Fifa president Gianni Infantino writing to all national associations offer £15m to accept the offer by 19 September, with the promise of a further £15m to follow.

But, following Thursday's vote, former Wales international McAllister said there was unity and a strong sense of feeling between all Uefa nations about what she called a "genuine existential threat to the game" and "a ridiculous proposal".

"Effectively it's a form of blackmail financially to present the national associations with such a tight time period to consider such a significant seismic proposal," said McAllister, who sits on Uefa's executive committee.

"I think that's part of the problem, but not the root of the problem. The root of the problem is trying to sell off parts of football to a private equity environment.

"This poses a genuine existential threat to the game because the minute you sell off part of the crown jewels of football, clearly private equity has very different objectives and motivations to those of us who are custodians of the game."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Uefa's boycott would cover all Fifa competitions - including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cup - and be triggered if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's proposals are voted through by member associations across the globe.

It would see a quarter of Fifa's members refusing to feature, including some of the world's biggest and most successful nations.

McAllister, who was elected to the position in 2023, admitted she hoped the boycotts do not come to pass – but warned it was not an empty threat.

"I feel optimistic they won't, because the reality is the powerhouse of world football is Europe," she told BBC Radio Wales Drive.

"So by taking the very powerful clear and categorical stance we've taken, hopefully we've given some confidence to the other confederations that they can follow suit, and that together we can defeat the proposal.

"This is not an empty threat because we have to be prepared to follow through on it, but I find it incredible that FIFA would consider pushing on with World Cups without European nations there."

McAllister also urged urged other governing bodies to push back on the controversial plans.

"I very much hope it will not come to a boycott and I find it hard to imagine that FIFA will want to push us into that situation and there's a number of reasons for that - one being the status of European nations in world football," McAllister told BBC Radio 4's PM show.

"A World Cup without Europe isn't a World Cup at all.

"There is now a timescale involved which can be rescinded. There are other confederations such as the Asian and Central and North American confederations who have already made their concerns known.

If the situation continues, I think the stance we've taken today will give some incentive to the rest of the world of football to stand up to this awful proposal."

She also accused FIFA, and Infantino, of being primarily motivated by money, and cited other examples of questionable interventions that has prompted scepticism within UEFA.

"I can only speak from a UEFA standpoint, but this isn't the only one that has caused us a problem.

"The overturning of the red card, the so-called FIFA peace prize, all of that has caused us quite some concern from a European standpoint."

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

Football Association of Wales chief executive Noel Mooney was among those to voice their concerns at the emergency meeting held virtually on Thursday.

There are now questions over the UK bid for the Women's World Cup in 2035. The joint bid by England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales was the only valid submission for the 48-team tournament, with confirmation of host status set to be delivered in November.

Prior to that, all four nations will be involved in play-offs for the 2027 World Cup.

McAllister, a former Wales captain, added: "We've got a lot of stages before that; you don't need to tell me how significant that is for Rhian Wilkinson and the girls.

"It's something that I've worked towards for all of my career in sports administration and as a player, but I don't think it will come to that because Europe really holds most of the cards in terms of how the World Cup can operate and its financial viability.

"Imagine a Women's World Cup without Spain, without England, without France, without Germany and the same would apply to the men."

title: Postgres Queues Actually Scale
description: Lessons learned from scaling Postgres-backed durable queues for users running tens of billions of workflows per month.
fullText:
The conventional wisdom around Postgres-backed queues is that they don't scale. To handle a large workload, you can't use Postgres, but instead need a dedicated queueing system like RabbitMQ + Celery or Redis + BullMQ. There's a reason people say this: queues really are a demanding workload for Postgres. At scale, thousands of workers are polling your queues table at the same time, creating contention and churning indexes. But with the right optimizations, Postgres can handle it. In this blog post, we'll show how we optimized Postgres-backed queues at scale, achieving 30K workflow executions per second across thousands of servers.

To make Postgres-backed queues work at all, the first problem to solve is contention between multiple workers dequeueing the same workflows. At a high level, the way Postgres-backed queues work is that clients enqueue workflows by adding them to a queues table, and workers dequeue and process the oldest enqueued workflows (assuming a FIFO queue). Naively, each worker runs a query like this to find the N oldest enqueued workflows, then dequeues them:

As soon as multiple workers run this query concurrently, contention arises. Every worker sees the same oldest queued workflows and attempts to dequeue them at the same time. But each workflow can only be dequeued by a single worker, so most workers will fail to find new work and have to try again. At a large scale, this contention creates a bottleneck in the system, limiting how rapidly tasks can be dequeued.

Fortunately, Postgres provides the primitive required to solve this problem: locking clauses. Here's an example of a query using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED:

Selecting rows in this way does two things. First, it locks the rows so that other workers cannot also select them. Second, it skips rows that are already locked, selecting not the N oldest enqueued workflows, but the N oldest enqueued workflows that are not already locked by another worker. That way, many workers can concurrently pull new workflows without contention. One worker selects the oldest N workflows and locks them, the second worker selects the next oldest N workflows and locks those, and so on.

Locking clauses make Postgres-backed queues possible (which is why SKIP LOCKED is one of those old Postgres tricks that keeps getting rediscovered). Without them, contention between workers prevents scaling beyond ~100 workflows per second. With them, Postgres can scale far further, but achieving that scaling requires more optimizations.

While locking clauses improve performance dramatically, we soon reached another contention-related bottleneck: at scale, dequeue operations would frequently fail with Postgres “Serialization Failure” exceptions and need to be retried. When dequeueing more than ~1000 workflows per second, the majority of dequeue operations encountered serialization failures, creating a performance bottleneck.

The culprit turned out to be Postgres transaction isolation levels. The dequeue transaction originally ran at REPEATABLE READ so it could support global queue limits like "run at most N workflows concurrently across all workers." Enforcing those global limits requires workers to share a globally consistent view of queue state, and REPEATABLE READ (in Postgres) guarantees that a transaction will operate on a fixed “snapshot” of the database as it was when the transaction started, and will not “see” the effects of concurrent transactions that complete while it is running.

The problem is that REPEATABLE READ becomes expensive at high concurrency. If multiple workers concurrently modify overlapping rows, Postgres aborts one of them with a serialization failure. At scale, workers spent more time retrying transactions than processing workflows.

The key realization was that the largest queues rarely used global flow control. At scale, users usually prefer local limits, such as "run at most 10 workflows per worker", which do not require cross-worker coordination.

So we made the isolation level conditional:

Queues with global flow control continue using REPEATABLE READ, while queues without it use READ COMMITTED, which eliminates serialization failures entirely and dramatically improves throughput.

With both locking clauses and a lower isolation level, contention virtually disappeared, even with thousands of workers. However, when running more than ~8000 workflows per second, we saw a new bottleneck: high CPU usage. This came from two seemingly unrelated places: the dequeue query itself and Postgres auto-vacuum. We found both sources shared the same root cause: inefficient indexes.

The workflow status table had several secondary indexes on it to speed up queries. One index was designed specifically for the dequeue query, indexing queue_name and status so Postgres could rapidly find all ENQUEUED workflows for a given queue:

Other indexes existed primarily for observability, for example, an index on parent workflow ID to enable efficient querying of workflow hierarchies:

At scale, these indexes were inefficient.

The dequeue index helps find all enqueued workflows, but doesn't return them in any particular order. As a result, when Postgres runs the dequeue query, it has to sort the returned workflows by timestamp to find the oldest enqueued workflows, increasing the query’s CPU usage.

Meanwhile, maintaining many indexes is costly. Every workflow status update (enqueue, dequeue, completion) requires updating every index. Moreover, after indexes are updated, Postgres autovacuum has to clean up outdated index entries. At high throughput, index maintenance and vacuuming consume a substantial fraction of database CPU.

The solution is to make indexes more selective.

First, we updated the main dequeue index so it not only returns all enqueued workflows for a particular queue name but also sorts them by priority and timestamp. Moreover, we converted it into a partial index that’s only maintained when workflow status is ENQUEUED.

This improves performance for two reasons. First, the dequeue query no longer needs an expensive sort step. Second, when the workflow is dequeued, Postgres can simply delete its index entry instead of maintaining it for the rest of the workflow’s lifetime, reducing maintenance and auto-vacuum cost.

We applied the same principle to most observability indexes. For example, the index on parent workflow ID is only maintained for workflows that actually have a parent:

Combined, these optimizations cut CPU usage dramatically, allowing queues to scale to over 30K workflows per second, or 80B per month.

If you like building scalable, reliable systems, we’d love to hear from you. At DBOS, our goal is to make Postgres-backed durable execution as simple and performant as possible. Check it out:

title: UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions

title: OpenAI revenue in July topped all of Q2 driven by GPT-5.6 release
description: OpenAI is trying to reassure employees that the business is healthy as competition emerges from Anthropic as well as a host of open-source players.
fullText:
As OpenAI chases rival Anthropic in the enterprise and tries to sustain growth in the face of new competition from cheaper open-source alternatives, the artificial intelligence company is seeking to reassure staffers that the business remains healthy.

In an internal meeting with employees on Wednesday, finance chief Sarah Friar and board chair Bret Taylor touted OpenAI's revenue growth and addressed competition with Anthropic, CNBC has learned. Friar said OpenAI's annualized recurring revenue in July exceeded the entire second quarter.

"And Q2 was no slouch," Friar said, according to a partial transcript of the meeting that was reviewed by CNBC.

Friar and Taylor said momentum was driven by the release of the company's GPT-5.6 series of models, its new enterprise agent called ChatGPT Work, and growing adoption of its AI coding tool, Codex.

OpenAI is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation as it gears up for a potentially massive IPO. The company faces a constantly changing competitive landscape that includes Anthropic and Google as well as a slew of so-called open-weight models out of China that can be accessed at much lower costs. Earlier this month, China's Moonshot AI unveiled Kimi K3, which claims it closes the gap with leading U.S. offerings and surpasses OpenAI and Anthropic's most capable systems on some benchmarks.

OpenAI has been racing to bring in new users, particularly enterprises and developers, in order to generate the revenue needed to help support its infrastructure spending plans, which are being funded by outside capital.

In February, OpenAI told investors that it plans to target roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. It's currently in discussions with Nvidia about a backstop of up to $250 billion that would help fund its plans to lease a massive new AI data center in Ohio, as CNBC reported earlier this week.

The staggering figures and the rapid rise of Anthropic, which surpassed OpenAI by valuation earlier this year, have raised questions about the durability of OpenAI's business. Anthropic said in May that its revenue run rate revenue topped $47 billion, up from the roughly $10 billion that it generated for all of 2025, as its Claude Code tool has become a huge hit with developers.

The Information reported in March that OpenAI had recently topped $25 billion in annualized revenue, citing a person with knowledge of the matter.

Taylor told employees on Wednesday that Anthropic had a strong start to the year, and he acknowledged that OpenAI had to play catch-up in the coding market. But he said he's encouraged by Codex's growth.

"You're seeing people who went deep on Claude Code, ended up with a very high bill, and started looking for an alternative," Taylor said at the meeting.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic confidentially filed for IPOs with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Neither company has disclosed additional details about when they plan to debut.
