title: We're making Chrome and the web safer in the AI Era
description: Chrome uses Gemini AI to automate vulnerability discovery, triage, and patching, accelerating updates to match modern security risks.
fullText:
How Chrome is using AI to improve vulnerability discovery, triage, and patching.

We’re living through a massive shift in the software security industry. Large Language Models (LLMs) are unlocking unprecedented capabilities for automated vulnerability discovery, scaling far beyond the limits of human security expertise, and requiring new approaches for staying ahead of attackers.

This means deploying AI models at scale to find and fix hundreds of security bugs, faster than ever, with the goal of achieving greater resilience and comprehensive remediation.

Some software bugs have security implications. While a purely functional bug might result in a frustrating UI freeze, a security bug (or vulnerability) can be used to build an exploit. Exploits allow attackers to perform malicious actions on a victim’s computer, such as reading private data, or controlling their machine without their knowledge.

Once a security bug enters the codebase, its life cycle proceeds as follows:

Our goal is for every one of these steps to happen as quickly as possible.

The Chrome Security team has been using LLMs for years. In 2023 we developed ways to use LLMs to increase security fuzzing coverage and performance. In 2024, we worked with Project Zero on Naptime, giving LLMs specialized tools for vulnerability research. And in 2025, we collaborated with DeepMind and Project Zero on Big Sleep, an AI vulnerability discovery agent that successfully found bugs in the V8 JavaScript engine and graphics stack.

In early 2026, we built an agent harness that used Gemini to find vulnerabilities across the broader Chrome codebase with higher efficiency and lower false positives. One of the bugs we found was a sandbox escape that would allow a compromised renderer to trick the browser into reading local files — a bug that quietly survived in our codebase for more than 13 years! For many of us, this moment cemented the potential of AI-powered vulnerability detection.

From there, we improved on our vulnerability finding agent harness by:

We’ve built all of this with safety in mind, and have put in place guardrails to mitigate the risk of AI behaving unexpectedly. Our AI analyzes source code strictly at rest, operating on locked-down machines that lack general internet access. We also utilize a dedicated setup for these internal scans that intercepts all network requests, employing strict allowlists based on the initiating application and destination, blocking any suspicious model activity. Furthermore, we never run models in an unrestricted mode, and we strictly limit our subagents from modifying the local system or accessing files outside of designated source code directories.

AI-powered vulnerability detection complements our existing security testing infrastructure. For example, fuzzing continues to be especially effective at finding bugs that arise from long-range interactions between disparate parts of our codebase, or those requiring a combination of seemingly unrelated operations.

We also want to continue to reward external researchers for their expertise and creativity in finding the most challenging and impactful vulnerabilities via the Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP). In early 2026, we saw a gradual increase in all categories of bug reports, but by March, the shift was apparent: we received more bug reports than we had in the entirety of 2025. This led us to change our VRP to focus researchers on bug submissions that are additive to what we are finding internally, and easily ingestible by our newly automated processing pipelines.

As we discover more security vulnerabilities with AI-powered tools, we’ve simultaneously used AI to scale and automate validating, triaging, and fixing bugs. Historically, triaging a single security report took anywhere from 5 to 30 or more minutes, and relied primarily on human expertise. We have been increasingly shifting our triage process towards an automated approach that blends rule-based systems with AI to increase throughput and accuracy.

The automated triage process is broken down into four key phases:

While it's hard to measure precisely, we estimate that this new process is saving hundreds of hours of developer time per month, allowing our team to focus on other security priorities.

Across Google, developers share the responsibility of prioritizing security fixes with the security team, but scaling bug discovery requires an equally scalable bug fixing process.

To achieve this, we rely on multi-agent workflows throughout:

At this point, we have LLMs generating candidate fixes for most vulnerabilities, dramatically increasing the rate of security fixes in recent Chrome releases:

Number of security bugs fixed in recent Chrome Stable release milestones

In the last two milestones, Chrome 149 and 150, we have fixed 1072 security bugs, surpassing the total number of security bugs fixed across the prior 23 milestones combined.

We have partnered closely with Google DeepMind and Project Zero for years, including on BigSleep and CodeMender. These tools are natively integrated into our continuous integration (CI) system, running every 24 hours across all CLs to proactively detect security bugs. This integration has yielded significant results: in May alone, we blocked over 20 vulnerabilities from reaching production, including a critical S1+ issue.

Once a fix has landed and is visible in the public open source codebase, attackers can start to reverse engineer and exploit the bug before the fix reaches users’ machines — so called "N-day" attacks. This is commonly referred to as the “patch gap.” Since fixes committed to the main “tree” typically take weeks to reach the Chrome Stable channel (what the vast majority of our users run), minimizing this patch gap is a critical part of our strategy.

Based on their severity, security fixes are merged directly from the main “tree” into the active Chrome stable release branch, which is continuously monitored to prevent new crashes or regressions. We are in the process of transitioning to a two-week cadence for major Chrome milestones, with weekly security updates. However, in the face of fast-moving, AI-powered attacks, our delivery cadence must accelerate even further. To meet this moment, we are piloting a shift to two security releases per week.

Even with this pace, proper public disclosure remains paramount. Every security bug that reaches Chrome Stable, regardless of whether it was discovered internally or reported externally, is documented and disclosed publicly as a standard best practice. We are working on automating the generation of release notes and CVE descriptions from security bug fixes to eliminate manual bottlenecks and shorten the window between vulnerability discovery and public disclosure.

In 2008, Chrome pioneered the concept of silent, background software updates: new binaries are automatically downloaded and staged on disk with minimal user intervention. At the next restart of the browser, the update would be applied and the user would be protected. However, compared to the 1–2 days it takes for triage, fix, test and release, the time spent waiting for the user to restart Chrome can be a significant contributor to N-day exploitation risk.

People have understandable reasons to delay restarting Chrome. A restart can be disruptive, requires scheduling in-between tasks, and is rarely the top priority at any given moment. To eliminate this friction, we are pioneering ways to shift the burden away from the user by:

Zero window auto-restart on macOS

Our long-term vision is a browser that is always up-to-date – continuously and dynamically patched, and automatically restarted during opportune periods of minimal disruption. While we’re working on this, you can keep your Chrome up to date by clicking on the update message in the top right corner.

For enterprise customers looking to keep Chrome up to date, we recommend that IT admins:

Beyond fixing individual security bugs, we’re also investing in the mitigation and elimination of entire classes of security bugs, as well as in preventing them from landing in the first place. With AI coding advancements, we believe there are exciting opportunities to accelerate projects that would have previously taken years, or never happened.

Chrome is executing on a two-layered memory safety strategy: hardening our runtime environment to neutralize legacy C++ vulnerabilities, while shifting to memory-safe languages for long-term architectural resilience.

The vast majority of the Chromium codebase remains in C++, making immediate toolchain and runtime mitigations our critical first line of defense. We have long prioritized memory-safety engineering at scale, deploying hardened standard template libraries and pioneering technologies like the MiraclePtr family to neutralize Use-After-Free (UAF) vulnerabilities. AI-powered vulnerability detection only reaffirms the need for such technology.

Our C++ defensive roadmap is focused on three pillars:

While C++ safety enhancements provide an immediate shield, we believe that runtime mitigations will hit diminishing marginal returns within the next few years. Runtime checks are inherently more expensive than compile-time guarantees, and even a heavily mitigated C++ binary requires rigid, performance-throttling sandboxing to comply with the Rule of Two.

The long-term solution is shifting the codebase towards memory-safe languages like Rust, focusing on the following core tenets:

In addition to Rust, we are also exploring options like implementing the browser’s top-level user interface using HTML, CSS, and TypeScript to further reduce dependencies on traditional C++ frameworks.

Bulk scanning of a code base cannot keep pace with Chrome’s high-traffic development velocity. To account for this, we’re also deploying AI-powered bug-finding capabilities to identify and prevent bugs as close to code submit-time as possible. Part of Chrome’s continuous integration (CI) and commit queue (CQ) pipeline, these defensive models automatically scan diffs to prevent new vulnerabilities by performing actions like suggesting spanification fixes, flagging dangling pointers, and enforcing numeric safety.

Additionally, a major challenge in large-scale software engineering is the “latent security issue.” Code that is safe and robust in isolation can be transformed into a critical vulnerability by an entirely unrelated, minor logic change elsewhere in the tree. By utilizing continuous, LLM-powered semantic analysis within the CQ, Chrome can intercept these compound risks before they land in the tree, catching the subtle or complex interactions that traditional static analysis misses.

Keeping the web safe involves more than just securing Chrome. Google has been a long-standing supporter of open source projects and communities to ensure better security outcomes for all users. Most recently, Google joined others in donating $12.5M to the Alpha-Omega project in support of enabling maintainers to have access to the tools and support they will need in order to respond quickly to vulnerability reports. Google was also a founding member of the Akrites project, which aims to lower the burden on upstream maintainers by providing a centralized clearinghouse for vulnerability reports and a security incident response team.

On the Chrome team, we feel this responsibility acutely — the Chromium Project is the largest open source project on the planet. To put the sheer scale of this challenge into perspective, Chrome has more than 2,300 third-party dependencies across Chromium and satellite projects like the V8 JavaScript engine, the BoringSSL cryptography library, and foundational graphics components like Skia, ANGLE, and Dawn. About 1,700 of those are shipped to users in some capacity, woven into a wide spectrum of products from Android devices to edge computing platforms and massive cloud enterprise stacks.

To keep these dependencies patched, we rely on automated vulnerability scanning pipelines. These pipelines ingest data from Google's internal feeds as well as several external monitoring feeds, including the U.S. government's National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and the open-source focused Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV) database.

Now more than ever, relying on reactive monitoring alone can leave a dangerous risk gap. Since the best way to stay on top of vulnerabilities and their patches is to keep third-party dependencies fresh, this year, we are starting to move all Chrome third-party dependencies onto automated update pipelines that proactively roll them to their latest upstream versions. Automation always requires guardrails, so we will also be using safety signals from projects such as Google’s Open Source Security Intelligence Platform (GOSSIP) to ensure that we are accounting for other risks in the third-party open source software ecosystem.

While this dramatic change in software security brought about by LLMs might be startling, an increase in bugs found and fixed is not a sign of failure. Every bug found and fixed is one less foothold for an attacker. But discovering and fixing a bug is only half the battle — we must also ship the fix and apply the update for users faster than adversaries can exploit the bug, and invest in projects that mitigate or eliminate classes of bugs through accelerated release cadences, dynamic patching, and opportune restarts, we are driving toward a browser that is continuously protected without disrupting the user.

The AI era has undeniably intensified the software security threat landscape, but by combining rapid deployment mechanisms with deep structural defenses, we are ensuring the advantage remains firmly with defenders. With this, Chrome and the broader web become safer with every update.

title: Flock's CEO Faced Me After Its Cameras Led to My Wrongful Stop
description: Flock CEO Garrett Langley sat down to discuss the errors that led to police stopping me and the growing fight over Flock's network of AI-powered surveillance cameras.
fullText:
Millions of people have seen the story of Flock cameras tracking me in a $155,000 Range Rover and subsequently four police officers surrounding my wife and me in a parking lot. Human error was involved, but Flock cameras working off the company’s AI tech compounded everything at an exponential rate.

Now on the latest episode of The Drivecast, Flock Safety Founder and CEO Garrett Langley sat down with me for a candid discussion about what happened to me and countless others in the last few years, the future vision for Flock amid the public backlash over privacy and Fourth Amendment concerns, the growing calls for regulation, and his previous comment that people who destroy or vandalize Flock equipment are “domestic terrorists.”

On a daily basis there’s reporting of cops misusing Flock’s tech to stalk people, which in turn ends up getting them arrested and sent to jail, misread situations taking place, arguments at city council meetings, and people targeting the automatic license plate readers and cutting them down, shooting them, covering them with trash bags and more. You might call this a hot topic, and somehow, I landed right in the middle of it.

New here? The Drivecast is The Drive‘s weekly podcast that takes you behind-the-scenes on the largest controversies, stories, and characters shaping the automotive industry along with the way our roads look today. Powered by The Drive‘s inside access, original reporting, exclusives, and insights, The Drivecast aims to make everyone an insider.

Listen to The Drivecast via Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or Amazon Music. Love it? Like it? Want to help? Leave a five-star review on your platform of choice to help get The Drivecast in front of more people. Have a suggestion, tip, request, or feedback? Drop us a line at feedback@thedrive.com. I promise, we read every single email.

Joel: Garrett, thank you for agreeing to come on the podcast. I know you’re extremely busy and there’s a lot of controversy at the moment surrounding Flock. You’re living your life on an airplane, even though you’re a family man. Just to get it out of the way and start, aside from a thank you, typically every executive we’ve had on this podcast, I kind of know them. I’ve worked in the industry for 15 years, so I usually know them, we’ve had a relationship. This is the first time I’ve ever met you. Given the podcast and everything, I have to ask: Are you a car enthusiast? Do you like cars? Do you care about driving? I’m genuinely curious.

Garrett: I hate to spoil it for your fans. I am not a car guy. Now, I have a deep appreciation for F1, and that’s more from an athletic standpoint. You look at the sheer engineering behind it—they’re optimizing every single millisecond, every single millimeter of the engine and of the design. But funny enough, up until two or three years ago, I was driving the same Toyota Prius that I’ve been driving since college. Everyone was like, “Why don’t you drive another car?” It works. It works really well. Gets me from A to B. It’s a great car. I wound up upgrading the dash to have Apple CarPlay, because the Toyota didn’t have it, so I retrofit that myself. But no, I get a hard time from some of my friends who love cars, saying that I should be more into cars. Between three kids, a wife, and a business, I’m trying to find time for the simpler things in life.

Joel: I can appreciate that. I didn’t really know what you were going to answer, because the reality is that you’re not a car company, you’re not a supplier of car parts or any of that stuff, so I think it was just context. By the way, a Prius, a Corolla, a Camry—there’s nothing really wrong with them. They’re not enthusiast cars, but to your point, if you’re looking for fuel-efficient, safe, reliable, get you from point A to point B, it’s hard to beat, specifically a Prius. The most recent one looks awesome.

Obviously, I have 99 million questions. There is zero chance we could ever cover all the topics today in the short period of time that you and I have together. I have to start with my situation, because that’s how we got here. There’s no way we could not discuss this. I don’t want to sit and belabor anything. You’ve read the stories, I’m sure you’re up to speed on what happened. I’ve written the stories, I’m well-versed with what happened. I’ve spent countless hours on the phone with your Chief Communications Officer, Josh—super nice guy.

As a recap, if you’re one of the millions of people that did not read the story or hear the podcast, a human error led to a police officer entering incorrectly an incomplete plate number into the National Crime Information Center database. That is managed by the FBI; that’s what all the police from across the nation pull from. That is also what gets fed into automatic license plate readers. Whether it’s Flock, Leonardo, or Axon, Garrett’s team doesn’t have its own database; they’re pulling from the FBI Criminal National Information Center database.

They were fed bad, partial, incorrect information. The system was told, “Go look for a license plate of 34DTM.” It was told to do that. It found it, but the problem was that the one it found—the one on my press car that week, a $155,000 Range Rover—also had a ’10’ in there. Flock saw it, the system saw it. It wasn’t asked about a ’10’, it wasn’t programmed to care about a ’10’, it was programmed to find the bone that it was asked to find. It did, and basically it fed it to the police. The local police then didn’t do the back-end loop, and they did not cross-check the actual plate. There was a photo of the plate, I saw it, they showed it to me, it had ’10’ on it. They either didn’t know what to do with it, they disregarded it, they didn’t enter it into the system. They looked at my plate, they didn’t understand the ’10’, and then they looked at my plate and thought I performed Grand Theft Auto, which I did not.

Basically, we had human error that led into Flock as a technology exponentially increasing the rate at which that error spread, but it wasn’t the source of the error. Then human error on the back end of that loop, not cross-referencing it. A compounding amount of issues at hand.

You can’t change human error; that’s not your job. What I am curious about is, I know Josh mentioned you guys talked to the FBI who manages NCIC, and he tried to talk to the LA police that entered the incorrect information. I’m curious from this situation: What will Flock as a company take away, what have they learned, and what changes will we learn from my edge case? We learn from edge cases.

Garrett: One, I appreciate you sharing and hitting on the facts, which is that there were a lot of things that went wrong. It’s easy to potentially try to aggregate that down to “Flock did this,” and a lot of mistakes happened to create this edge case. Sadly, you weren’t the first person who’s had an edge case, and to your point, Joel, the biggest issue remains this national database at the FBI called NCIC, and how archaic its structure is. There’s no feedback loop mechanisms; it’s really just a static comma-separated file.

We’ve tried to build around it. We have this concept called “suppression.” A local agency—let’s take Atlanta, where I live—might see that there’s a stolen plate out of California, but it’s already been resolved because it’s a rental car or a dealer car. They can, in Flock, suppress that: “Never alert us on that for the next year.” That’s to get around the fact that they can’t force another agency to remove it from NCIC.

Ideally, the way it would work is if enough agencies—let’s call it one, two, or three—flag a tag as no longer valid or a bad entry, it should just get removed. Or at least it should get pushed more aggressively by the FBI. For us, we maintain a productive relationship with the FBI. They obviously play a critical role in broader public safety, and I’m hopeful that they’ll see there’s an opportunity to make something like NCIC, which is an important tool not just for companies like Flock, but for police departments to work together, start to make some enhancements to modernize what’s a central part of our policing system.

Joel: I’m curious because you said something I hadn’t heard yet, whether talking to the chief of police or Josh. When my situation occurred, one of the things I learned from my local police that this all went down with is they asked me where I was going to drive the car, if I was going to drive to other suburbs. I said yes. They warned me that other police officers might be trained differently—Minneapolis might be more aggressive, they might show up with guns drawn, which mine didn’t.

They warned me that I have the case number and my police officer’s name that went through everything with me, and they’re like, “In Plymouth, you have a safety net now; you’re not going to get flagged. But if you go into another suburb with Flock, it’s going to flag you again because it’s pulling from the NCIC.” If Plymouth had done the suppression thing you just mentioned, that doesn’t translate to the Minneapolis Police Department.

Garrett: No, it only impacts Plymouth, because we don’t necessarily want to make a decision on behalf of Minneapolis or Los Angeles. We very much have this structural viewpoint that local decisions should stay local. Plymouth made a decision to suppress that, that’s their right to do that, but that doesn’t impact Minneapolis’s setup.

Joel: Do you believe that in this situation, Plymouth police quickly realized—”quickly” is a relative term in the scheme of life—in the scheme of that day, my wife will tell you so, but do you think that, to your point about the NCIC database, Plymouth police told me the only ones in the situation that could have updated that partial plate in the system would be the officer’s unit? In this case, it was the LA Sheriff’s Department, Malibu Lost Hills station. They’re the only ones that can update that issue. Do you think that as you are talking with NCIC and the FBI about how to modernize the system, it should be able to allow Plymouth police, if they run this down and talk to LA and figure out the situation, to correct this? We shouldn’t have to have this weird loop of Jaguar having to call LA.

Garrett: A proposed solution would be one where—let’s make it you and me so it’s easier and fewer words. Garrett puts in a tag “FEDER” as a stolen car. If Joel says, “Wait a second, I just pulled that person over, that’s not valid anymore,” you should have the ability to say, “I think this should be removed.”

Then to me, I should have some clock—called a day, a week—to say, “No, Joel, you are wrong, I want to keep this.” That to me makes a lot more sense, where you have the ability to say, “Hey, I should delete this,” and I go, “Okay, well I can either let it disappear because I’m not going to fight it, or I could choose to say there’s a reason why that you might have misunderstood.”

I agree with you, there needs to be more collaboration. That’s how more modern systems work. Similarly on our side, I think to your point…

Joel: To be clear, in this situation where I’m Feder and you’re Garrett with the license, are you talking about you as Flock, or you as the FBI NCIC?

Garrett: Us as police departments. Let’s make it easier: I’m LA County, I enter in FEDER as this stolen car. You’re Plymouth and you’re like, “I don’t think it’s stolen anymore, this looks normal.” You should be able to say, “I think it needs to be deleted.” As LA County, I should have a day or a week to say, “No, it is really stolen,” or it automatically gets deleted and removed from the list.

Inevitably what happens is, let’s take the rental car example: A car is reported stolen by the rental car agency. I’m LA County and I put it in NCIC. But then, low and behold, the car was returned a month later. It was not stolen, someone just forgot to return it or something. To me, there’s either an expiration—if you look at the way the Flock system works, which is a little bit different than NCIC, we require an expiration period. You can’t just put something into a list forever. It either is going to be there for 7 days, 30 days, 90 days—you have to define this expiration. I think that would also be a meaningful and positive change to NCIC, to have a 7-day or 30-day max expiration period so that you don’t wind up with this stale data in the system like you experienced.

Joel: Last question on this topic. Flock has an expiration, but NCIC doesn’t. So in this case, let’s make believe in some timeline that didn’t happen and my wife got a manicure that day. She would have been much happier. If 34DTM had been in the system and not gotten pulled over, you’re pulling from NCIC, it wasn’t in the Flock database. You said there are expirations, it can’t be searching forever. How does that work if it’s not expiring out of the NCIC?

Garrett: Here’s a good example: Let’s take Plymouth. Let’s say Plymouth has reasonable suspicion that Feder’s license plate was associated with a residential burglary. They could create on their local version a hot list entry to say, “Hey, this is our Plymouth-only hot list.” There’s NCIC, and we force an expiration on the local level. I think it would be great if NCIC had a similar expiration requirement of, let’s call it a week or a month, so that as a criminal investigator, every month you have to reconfirm, “Yes, I am still looking for this car, it is still an active investigation.” I think that would help a lot. It puts more onus on law enforcement, but your story is a prime one of why the extra work by the law enforcement agency is worth it. It’s not that much work relative to your experience.

Joel: Got it. Let’s pivot from my experience into the future of here and now, and where we go from here, but staying on my topic a little as a joiner setup.

Josh made mention—and it’s all over your website—that there’s a 99% success rate. I don’t want to sit here and question that, so let’s use that in this scenario. You guys are doing about—these are round numbers to be clear, because they’re big—20 billion reads a month. 20 billion reads a month and a 99% success rate means there’s a 1% error rate, misread rate, call it whatever you want to call it. 1% of 20 billion, which is a huge number, is a huge number. I was one of them. Now, I wasn’t a misread, to be clear, but it was an error situation with a bad outcome that ended up with an outcome we don’t want.

What exactly are we doing, what’s Flock doing, what’s being done to bring down that 1% error rate so we’re not at 200 million? Which sounds like an immense number—not an immense number when you have 20 billion, but it’s still a big number.

Garrett: Your experience wasn’t even a misread; that’s a flaw in the error. The math you used—we don’t need to debate it, but what I would articulate is that doesn’t express the false positive rate, which is actually what you should be worried about. A false positive rate would say we read a license plate, FEDER, we’re confident it’s FEDER, and it’s stolen according to NCIC, so we send an alert.

It’s not just a function of how accurate we are, but how confident in our accuracy. There’s an important detail in how the system works, because technology will never be perfect, just like human eyes aren’t perfect. The question is what redundancies and what guardrails are you building into the system to prevent and reduce the likelihood of something bad happening.

In our case, let’s say it’s FEDER, and we’re 99% confident it’s an F, 99% on an E, 99% on a D, 99% on an E, and we’re only 80% confident that R is an R. We don’t send the alert.

Joel: Is that how it’s set up today?

Garrett: Yes, that’s how it works today. That’s an important detail because we will save that image, and we will store that under a certain confidence interval, but there is a very high bar for us to notify a local law enforcement officer in their MDT, in their patrol vehicle, of an NCIC alert. We have to be very confident, because even though we do the training and say you need to human verify this, and even though we do the training and say you need to double-check NCIC that there’s an active warrant, even though we do all that training, we know that humans are going to make mistakes.

We know that for many people, myself and yourself included, being pulled over by an officer is scary. It is. I’ve been pulled over before, I’ve sped, it happens. It’s scary, your heart races. We want to put that at a 0% likelihood that there is a wrongful traffic stop.

Joel: What’s the threshold? You said 80%, 99%. What’s the threshold that it has to be?

Garrett: I don’t think the number matters as much, because if I told you it’s 50%, you’d say, “What does that mean?” Here’s a way to think about it: It’s less than one in a million alerts that an officer says, “I’m not sure if that’s right.” Less than one in a million. To me, it’s incredibly low. Now, should it be one in a billion? Sure, that’s an interesting tradeoff.

For me, to your point, I want the OCR or the character recognition to be as good as possible. I would argue we have the best license plate reading camera in the world. We definitely are the largest provider of it in the world, so we probably have the best. For me, I think we’ve built these multiple redundancies to prevent—your situation is hard because I can’t control NCIC. What I can control is a wrongful traffic stop due to an OCR misread, and that I think we do have a lot of control over.

Joel: That’s a great transition to some broader questions about where we are today, what’s happening, and where we go in the future. I’d like to start with the future. You’re the man behind Flock. You founded it, you’re in charge of it, you’re the CEO. What is your vision for the future?

For context, I live in Plymouth, Minnesota. There are 18 cameras in Plymouth right now; that’s not every street corner today. Now, there are cities that have a lot more than that, and cities that have a lot less. My question is, what’s your vision for the future? Is there a Flock camera on every street corner, in every school? I know you guys are introducing new technology that’s not just cameras on top of streetlights. What’s your vision for the future, where are we going?

Garrett: One, thank you for the chance to talk about this, because I’ve spent the last decade of my life thinking about this. Just like you, I’m a father of three kids. My primary objective as a father is to keep them safe. They’ve got to be safe. Then I’ve got to make sure they’re educated, that they’re good people, productive members of society. But if they’re not safe, everything else starts to crumble. I think that’s true for a lot of kids. That lack of feeling safe starts to lead to these erosions of society.

If I zoom all the way out, we’ve always thought about crime and safety in two big buckets. You’ve got one bucket, which is emotional crime—crimes of passion. I hate to say it, we’re not going to stop those. They’ve been around for thousands of years. However long humans have been around, we have unfortunately been having passionate crimes, which is horrible. So we’ve got to solve those, but we’re not going to stop them.

The opportunistic crime, though—that’s actually very controllable. The majority of crime, let’s call it 95% to 99% of crime, is truly opportunistic. “I walk by your car, I believe I can get away with stealing it, so I choose to steal it.” That is the thought process.

What we’ve noticed is in certain places like San Francisco, four years ago, you could get away with almost any crime. Then two or three years ago, Mayor Breed and Mayor Lurie said, “Flock, we need help. It’s too easy to be a criminal, and our businesses are leaving, our people are leaving. This isn’t working for us.”

We deployed hundreds of license plate readers, we deployed our drones, we deployed our real-time crime center software to make officers more efficient. Now it’s one of the safest cities in America. Mayor Lurie has one of the highest approval ratings of any major city mayor—he might actually have the highest, last I checked.

For me, the future is a future where more cities look like San Francisco, where crime is incredibly hard to get away with—so hard that people just choose not to do it. That might seem like a distant future, but it’s happening in San Francisco. I think we’re going to do the same thing in Oakland. We’re in 7,000 cities today, and I’d like to get us to all 17,000 cities in America and create that future, because it’s quite doable. Whatever technology we need to build to help get there while maintaining our local societal norms is what we’re planning to do. That might sound crazy, but I said it 10 years ago, and now it’s really happening at scale. It’s a pretty exciting time.

Joel: Societal norms—you mentioned that. I want to be very clear, we’re not a political podcast, that’s not where we’re going to go, and I don’t really want to get into that here on the podcast. But societal norms—at one end of the spectrum, we’ve got people that are like, “If we have these on every corner, we’re going to have a dragnet map of your life without a warrant, and a Fourth Amendment violation.” Where do you fall on this whole topic of where Flock sits today, where the company sits tomorrow as you expand, and the warrantless Fourth Amendment concern—people’s concern of you doing a digital map of their entire life without a warrant?

Garrett: People tend to have three concerns or three questions about the company: privacy, constitutionality, and accountability.

You mentioned the constitutional one. That one’s pretty cut and dry. You and I don’t get to pick what’s a constitutional violation and what’s not. We have judges, we have elected officials, there’s a process for that. We follow the law, we follow the Constitution. So far, in our belief and what will be for a long time, the courts have deemed this is not a warrantless search; this is a valid product as it relates to the Fourth Amendment. So I don’t see any change there.

On the privacy one, though, there’s some real questions that we ask as well. Here’s a good example: Before I started Flock, this type of ALPR data was stored in perpetuity. It was resold for commercial purposes by repo trucks to insurance providers. It was pretty nasty, in my opinion. We were one of the first companies to say there’s going to be a 30-day default retention, and we aren’t going to sell the data.

I’ll tell you an interesting stat: We solved just over a million crimes last year on the Flock system in partnership with local law enforcement. If I told you that if we reduce the 30-day retention to 14 days, 30% fewer crimes would be solved—so roughly 300,000 more victims without justice—would you make that tradeoff?

Before you answer—I won’t make you answer that one on the spot—my point would be you and I shouldn’t pick. Actually, the Mayor of Plymouth and the City Council should make that decision, because that’s a fair tradeoff. We elect people who we believe match our values to make these very difficult, non-black-and-white questions. There’s no answer there, because you could go down with something like Flock and say, “We like the idea of Flock, but we only want to focus on Amber Alerts and Silver Alerts.” So there’s zero retention of the data, just alerts. I’d say, “Okay, you’re going to get about 50% of the value of the system, but if that’s what you want in Plymouth, great, we’d love to help you, but you’re still going to be safer.” Now, you’re going to be less safe than San Francisco, but that’s an option.

For us, we don’t want to push our opinion as individual citizens. I live in Atlanta, you live in Plymouth. We just wish that more elected officials would do their research, do their homework, form an opinion, engage the community, and then set a standard that makes sense for them.

Joel: Let’s go down the elected officials route; this was actually one of my questions. I’ve seen Congress members—not one, not two, a couple of them now—post on Instagram about introducing bills that would withhold federal funding from municipalities that would use Flock. I’m curious what you make of that. None of these, by the way, to my knowledge, have been introduced as of the time of this recording; they’ve all just been discussions, but they’re being thrown out there. It is being talked about.

Garrett: At the highest level, nothing would make me happier than if we had state-by-state regulation on this type of technology. That to me is so crystal clear, because the lack of regulation on this type of technology just shows that our elected officials need to move faster than they have historically. I’m not the first person to say that. That’s the case with technology in general, where we just tend to build and innovate as a country faster than we can regulate. That’s generally okay, but in this case, they’re behind.

The proposition of federal defunding of roughly, in this case, 80% of police departments because they use technology to keep their community safe is completely… I don’t know how that’s logical to people when there are so many better alternatives to regulation.

I think that there is a very low likelihood that anyone is that irresponsible to even propose such legislation. When it has been discussed in the past—which was about six months ago—it barely made it out of someone’s mouth before it was killed. I would just challenge those Congress folks, men and women, instead of being critical of the men and women who work tirelessly to keep us safe and the tools they need to be effective, maybe we should actually just talk about what guardrails are necessary for everyone to feel good about what’s required.

To me—and Joel, I don’t know if you agree, I hope you do—I think it’s crazy that in America today, there’s a 50/50 chance of getting away with homicide. That seems completely unacceptable as a society. Banning tools that allow us to drive clearance rates higher…

I say this because in Atlanta, where I live, there was a woman who was violently murdered in the middle of the night in Piedmont Park, our biggest park, five years ago, and that case is still cold. You know why? Because even though there were cameras, the cameras weren’t working. If those cameras were working, that woman’s family would have justice. They don’t today, and I think that’s horrible. We should not be comfortable with that as a society, and I know in Atlanta we are not.

Joel: We talked about Congressmen and elected politicians. I have to get your viewpoint on what you make of the public pushback, or towns canceling contracts, or not renewing contracts. By the way, I want to be clear on the podcast, I actually felt there was a lot of miss and/or shoddy reporting on a couple of the towns that “canceled” contracts, because they actually were set to expire and didn’t get renewed, and I dug into that. As a journalist, it irked me. But that’s not the point.

I am curious, what’s your viewpoint on the public pushback, towns either canceling or not renewing contracts? Flock’s not something that people use; it’s not something I use. It’s not something I’m opting into like iCloud or whatever, it’s something you have to accept, because you’re driving down the road and I didn’t opt into it like I do with my AirPods or my phone. I’m guessing that’s kind of some of the public pushback here when we were talking about the whole map and dragnet. We discussed your take on that, but I’m curious about your viewpoint on this public pushback and towns canceling or not renewing contracts.

Garrett: It’s a really interesting phenomenon, because in most businesses—I’ll take the case of your business—if one of your advertisers or one of your partners chooses not to renew, it’s not a headline. When you add a new advertiser, it’s not a headline. It’s been interesting because we’ve added probably 10 times the number of customers that are new than who have not renewed their service in the last 90 days, but you won’t read that in the headlines, right? Because it’s not an interesting story to say, “Oh, this city adopted Flock.” It’s only interesting to say, “This city has paused their service” or canceled it.

What’s also interesting to me is the media hasn’t reported on the dozens of agencies who paused their service, saw crime go up, and have now turned them back on. It’s just interesting. I don’t know why, but to your point, some are turning it off, and that’s their choice. What they will find is they will be less safe, and then they will call us back, whether it’s in a week, 30 days, or a year. We have a demonstrable impact on public safety, and some cities have tried the experiment and it fails, and they have an obligation to keep their citizens safe.

Joel: Final question before we go into a hot round of however long we have left: You’re a private company, and you’re the middleman between the public and the government. You’re helping the police, but you’re not a supplier, you’re a service. You’re selling a service, it’s a SaaS. It’s a subscription service, and if they stop paying, like we just discussed, you turn it off; they no longer have access to the service. But it’s a service to the government, but you’re serving the government in between the public, because you’re taking pictures of the public’s license plates or whoever’s running through, and then it’s going to the government. You’re not a government-owned entity. It’s not a common place thing in this type of situation.

Garrett: This is a really interesting question, so it gives me a chance to hit on a few points. One, and this has been misreported as well—hopefully you can help me get this word out—we do not own the data, the government owns the data. We don’t have access to it. We are the custodian, and the reason why we did this goes back to my example.

We got questions from our customers like, “We’re used to just buying equipment.” I said, “Well, how’s that going for you? Are you experts in camera installation, camera maintenance?” My Atlanta example before is a prime example of what happens when we ask our government to do too much. Law enforcement is really good at one thing, which is hopefully solving crime. That’s what we ask them to do. They’re not necessarily good at building cameras, designing cameras.

It’s important to know our customer owns the data. I would actually agree with you, one of the hardest parts about building this business is that the last company to go public in this space was 25 years ago. That’s not every measure for success by any means—you can build a great business that doesn’t go public—but when you think about other industries that have seen the sheer benefit of technology, we’ve left behind local government. No one wants to service local government.

This is one of the reasons why, as you and I talked about, this is a controversial company. I appreciate that. We are not setting up the next generation of entrepreneurs to get excited about working with local government when, honestly, they need more innovation, local government needs more technology. It’s hard, it’s really hard, but I think it’s worth it.

Joel: Let me ask you—Josh and I, if anyone’s cutting in now and hasn’t heard this, Josh is the Chief Communications Officer I talked to, and he’s been in a couple of our stories—he did make a mention of something you just noted, that you guys don’t own the data, it’s stored on AWS (Amazon Web Services), and that it’s bucketed by municipalities, and certain municipalities can have sharing with other municipalities.

We see in the news countless examples of whether it’s in Texas, or your home area, Georgia—bad actors, bad police misusing your system, stalking women, stalking ex-girlfriends and their family members, checking a certain license plate 179 times in a certain period of time, etc. Obviously, there are audit logs—Josh told me about this and this is how people get caught with audit logs.

I am curious, do you guys have multi-factor authentication? The reason I ask this is because even my iCloud and my Meta accounts have multi-factor authentication, and it makes it easier to track who that actual person is in the audit log and the audit trail to get caught. Does that make sense?

Garrett: Yes, so let’s hit on a few of these. As a matter of fact, we do. We do require multi-factor authentication, which is a step in the right direction. We’ve had that for years. Now, we used to not require it, it used to be optional, and the main reason why being if you’re a town of 10 sworn officers, you’re unlikely to be offering both a laptop and a mobile device that are government-issued. To do proper multi-factor authentication, you need to have multiple devices.

We’ve evolved our thinking and said any version of MFA is better than no MFA, so we will just mandate it now, which we’ve now done.

To your point on auditability and accountability, yeah, I actually think this is a problem more broadly in law enforcement—that we’re one of the only systems that actually has auditing and has abnormal behavior detection in it. All these cases you see happening are because our system is flagging, “That’s pretty weird.” It’s not necessarily illegal—innocent until proven guilty—but a criminal investigation should have occurred. I wish more state regulations pushed that every system law enforcement uses needed to have this level of sophisticated auditing and abnormal detection.

We’ve got to do more there. The only other point I’d add, Joel, is I was just earlier today on the phone with one of our customers in Ohio, and they were sharing a success story on an ICAC crime—Internet Crimes Against Children. Let’s think about society, let’s think at the bottom of society, some of the most evil people. He was sharing with me this story of how the case was completely cold, but then they were using Flock and they found the individual, they’ve arrested him. You’re not going to go to the 5:00 news and talk about an ICAC case; it’s not appropriate, people don’t want to hear about this stuff.

I have the benefit of hearing from my customers every single day of these incredibly heroic stories where they found that one needle in the haystack. I wish the media and I wish our customers did an even better job of selling that story, but I also can appreciate that as a society, we don’t want to hear about all the evil that’s out there, and we rely on local law enforcement to catch those bad people, and state law enforcement and federal law enforcement to catch those bad people.

The abuse is a problem. We need to continue to get that down to zero. Any level of abuse is unacceptable, to be very clear, but I don’t think we should miss the fact that over a million cases were solved last year with this technology, and the level of abuse is incredibly low relative to that.

Joel: I would be remiss—this was not in my original rundown, but I know you’re in the news all the time, you are, and Flock is as well. The fact that we’re sitting here and that we were brought together because of my situation that I experienced, I’m sure in the comments on the internet, people would skewer me if I did not ask the question.

Weeks ago—the last month’s kind of a blur with everything that’s happened—weeks ago, a journalist asked you a question about what you make of the people that are cutting down, shooting, etc., the Flock cameras. You gave a passionate response that used the word “domestic terrorists” or something like that. I know since then you’ve apologized for it, I’ve seen that video as well and that coverage. If we went back in time, I have to ask about it.

Garrett: Look, I clearly could have done a better job delineating between individuals who commit felonies—where, to be clear, destruction of government property, destruction of property, is a felony in many states. We can change the law, but currently the law says that if you vandalize something, that’s illegal. To individuals that are promoting breaking the law, I just find that confusing. We’re a company that, by and large, by design from our founding, was that people shouldn’t break the law. I don’t know why that’s controversial, that I don’t agree with breaking the law.

Now, what I got wrong, and what I apologized for to your point, a comment that I made 18 months ago, was not clearly separating that viewpoint from organizations like the ACLU or the EFF, and now groups like DeFlock, who are trying to make sure their voice is heard. I think that’s great. We might disagree on some of the details, but I think that’s perfectly fine. Just like I have a right as a business owner, as a father, to share my voice, to vote, to do that—I think that’s great.

I didn’t delineate that enough, and I should have been clearer that I think committing a felony is bad, and I think voicing your opinion is A-OK, it’s great. I actually think the more of it, the better. I think people should be more involved in local politics. I don’t know what your level of engagement is in Plymouth, but I can tell you that you have an ability to influence what’s happening, and it also impacts your life more than you think than state and federal politics.

Joel: I really appreciate your time. I really appreciate your team setting this up, I appreciate you coming on the podcast. You’re definitely welcome to come back. I would love to continue the conversation another time in the future. I think there’s so much more that you and I could talk about in terms of technology, what your company can do, what other companies are doing, the differentiation points, and I’d welcome the opportunity.

Garrett: Awesome, awesome. Thank you very much, appreciate it, and we’ll talk to you soon.

title: AMD Posts Linux Patches for HDMI 2.1 Auto Low-Latency Mode "ALLM" & VRR
description: Following AMD posting AMDGPU patches for HDMI 2.1 FRL support after the HDMI 2.1 open-source support was long blocked by the HDMI Forum, as part of working toward a complete HDMI 2.1 implementation in this AMD Linux driver it was followed by HDMI 2.1 Display Stream Compression (DSC) support
fullText:
AMD Posts Linux Patches For HDMI 2.1 Auto Low-Latency Mode "ALLM" & VRR

Following AMD posting AMDGPU patches for HDMI 2.1 FRL support after the HDMI 2.1 open-source support was long blocked by the HDMI Forum, as part of working toward a complete HDMI 2.1 implementation in this AMD Linux driver it was followed by HDMI 2.1 Display Stream Compression (DSC) support. Now the latest on the AMDGPU HDMI 2.1 enabling path is enabling Auto Low-Latency Mode (ALLM) as well as HDMI Variable Rate Refresh!
Out today are the patches from AMD for enabling HDMI 2.1's Auto Low-Latency Mode in the AMDGPU Linux driver. HDMI ALLM allows your computer (or game system) to inform the display device to turn on the "Game Mode" to optimize for faster gaming speeds. The intent is on reducing latency and lag for a faster gaming experience with modern TVs / monitors.
With the AMDGPU driver patches, HDMI 2.1 ALLM is enabled when the set content-type is "Game" per user-space requests or when "Gaming-VRR" variable rate refresh is enabled.
The other exciting element is the HDMI 2.1 VRR support with DisplayPort VRR having already been long supported by the AMDGPU driver. Another exciting milestone for Linux gamers with AMD Radeon graphics to finally enjoy HDMI 2.1 VRR.
The patches are now out for review on the mailing list. Time is getting tight though for the DRM-Next cut-off for getting this into the upcoming Linux v7.3 merge window, so we'll see if it makes it for the next kernel cycle during the back half of August or if it will be pulled back until v7.4. In any case great seeing more of the AMDGPU HDMI 2.1 support coming together.

title: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant
description: Romania, Bulgaria and Serbia are also grappling with the effects of a series of prolonged heatwaves and low rainfall.
fullText:
Hungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said.

The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it.

Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week.

Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer.

The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania.

Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment.

A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited.

In Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power.

The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.

It is the fasting warming content, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires.

Romania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600cm per second. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500cm per second by Tuesday.

The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries.

The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea.

The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia.

And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth.

They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib.

Shipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania.

Passengers had been running low on food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, and another boat that was called in to help was unable to get close enough.

"I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency.

It is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube.

Serbian hydrologist Dejan Vladiković said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring.

He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September.

Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C.

Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected.

Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory, leading to hundreds of thousands of evacuations.

title: The parasite panic didn't stop thousands of nutrition experts from chowing down on salad
description: Still skipping your lunch salad over cyclospora fears? Doctors and nutritionists didn't miss their daily dose of leafy greens at a recent conference.
fullText:
At a conference, I saw doctors and dietitians enjoying salad, despite the cyclosporiasis outbreak.

They told me the risk doesn't warrant swearing off fresh produce, a key part of a healthy diet.

It made me feel safer about eating salads at home — with a few extra precautions.

As a health reporter, I've spent weeks in the trenches of the cyclosporiasis outbreak, trying to decipher the gastrointestinal gamble of eating fresh produce right now.

I've talked to doctors, tracked case numbers, and tuned into FDA briefings all in the pursuit of one question: Is a piece of iceberg lettuce an accident waiting to happen right now?

Then I took a train to Washington, DC, for Nutrition 2026, one of the country's biggest nutrition conferences, where 3,000 doctors, dietitians, and food science researchers gathered to discuss healthy — and safe — eating.

The first thing that caught my attention wasn't research-related; it was lunch. Almost everyone was eating chopped salad.

A few people skipped the greens — some drenched their salad dressing on lower-risk veggies like cucumbers instead — but by and large, the nutrition community seemed OK with leafy greens.

I was a little surprised. The cyclosporiasis outbreak is still very much ongoing. To date, more than 11,000 people in 46 states have been sickened with a parasite that causes explosive diarrhea. The FDA, CDC, and local health officials recently expanded their investigation to include more states, and they are still working to trace the outbreak's sources and ultimately contain it.

So why were these health experts eating salad? I spent the weekend badgering dietitians and food safety experts about how they're deciding what's OK to put on their plates. Here's everything I learned about eating healthy food with less anxiety.

Cyclospora crops up in our food supply every summer.

How does it get there? Sorry to tell you… it's usually poop. Plants grow in the ground, and animals poop there. We water crops with water that may contain poop. And ultimately, fruits and veggies are picked, handled, and transported by many people before they get to your plate, and not everyone washes their hands for the full length of Happy Birthday like we were all taught in kindergarten.

While health officials still haven't identified the exact source of the current outbreak, iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms remains under investigation, and questions remain about lettuce, herbs, and berries.

Products like bagged salads can be particularly problematic because greens are mixed and then spread across large batches, allowing any hitchhiking contaminants to travel far and wide.

I talked to over a dozen dietitians, doctors, and researchers over the weekend.

No one was particularly nervous about the greens at the buffet — not because they thought the outbreak was overblown. They simply understood that the absolute risk of getting sick from any given salad remains relatively low, while the health benefits of eating vegetables remain overwhelming.

"The anxiety people feel around this outbreak is understandable," Alyssa Pike, a registered dietitian and a senior manager of food safety at the International Food Information Council, told me. She's still eating salads herself, but paying close attention to recalls and avoiding products that health officials are actively investigating.

"If you aren't comfortable eating lettuce right now," she said, "the good news is there are lots of other types of produce."

Psychologist William Hallman, who researches food risk communication at Rutgers University, said the people attending the conference have a very different relationship with the food system (and food safety) than the average consumer.

They're more familiar with how outbreaks are investigated, how contamination spreads, and how to interpret evolving public health guidance.

"In short, many consumers are avoiding salads not because the statistical risk of Cyclospora infection is high, but because the public messaging around the outbreak has been contradictory and difficult to interpret," Hallman told me. "People want to feel in control of the food choices they make for themselves and their families."

That uncertainty has become one of the defining features of this outbreak. For non-experts, cutting back on greens offers only a limited sense of comfort amid a lot of confusion.

Investigators initially thought they had found cyclospora in a Taylor Farms lettuce sample, only to later determine the result was a false positive, leading to mixed messages about what is or isn't safe to eat.

Still, the overwhelming evidence points to the iceberg lettuce, which originated in Mexico, as the source of the outbreak. Since it's been voluntarily recalled from grocery store shelves and restaurants like Taco Bell, consumers can feel safer about lunch.

Avoiding foodborne illness is tough.

The day I arrived at the conference, cyclospora wasn't the only hazard going around. The CDC announced an outbreak of Salmonella in eggs. As I was writing this, the USDA announced a recall of more than 12,000 pounds of bacon.

While I personally skipped lettuce on my trip, I was definitely loading up on scrambled eggs at the free hotel breakfast (so far, so good), and bacon wasn't on the menu. The alternative of eating ultra-processed convenience foods all weekend, plus the gallons of coffee I need to do journalism, would have led to a different kind of digestive disaster.

Back home in New York, greens have long been a part of my weekly meal prep. They still are — I've just switched to buying local, since the scale of the outbreak makes it more likely to be tied to a large distributor than to a small farm.

Holding off the iceberg lettuce this week might make sense if you're worried about this outbreak, but it doesn't mean you should swear off salad forever. If your risk tolerance is higher, you can still eat leafy greens, particularly if you know the source or if you're in an area with fewer cases of this particular illness.

If there's one thing I learned from the weekend, it is that there is no perfect way to eat. That's what the whole conference was about: how to advance the latest cutting-edge nutrition science on what's good for our bodies, while also aligning it with how we actually live our lives.

The takeaway: Be cautious, but don't panic. Stress can give you diarrhea, too.

title: Army conducts first overseas test of 'Hammer of the Gods' weapon-disrupting system
description: The Army says its "Hammer of the Gods" electronic warfare system completed its first overseas maritime test, disrupting navigation signals used by enemy precision weapons.
fullText:
The U.S. Army on Sunday revealed it has tested a new warfare system overseas designed to covertly scramble the navigation signals used by enemy precision weapons, making it harder for adversaries to accurately strike targets from long distances while avoiding detection.

The electronic system, dubbed "Hammer of the Gods," was tested at sea off the U.S. West Coast for the first time in mid-July as part of the Project Convergence Capstone 6 (PC-C6) experiment.

While land-based versions have been demonstrated over the past two years, the exercise marked the official debut of the maritime variant, the Army said.

The portable signal disruptor can reportedly blind enemy to several precision-guided weapons such as long-range artillery, guided missiles and cruise missiles.

Ukraine's Battlefield Is Transforming The Future Of Nato

The radio signals specifically jam positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) signals, including GPS data, that precision weapons rely on to navigate accurately.

Without reliable PNT data, weapon accuracy drops sharply, increasing the likelihood of delayed missions and missed targets.

The system also creates a resilient communications network that allows friendly forces to stay connected despite heavy electronic jamming.

Report Warns Russia Using Shadow Fleet To Probe Nato Drone Defenses

It links military devices together, so troops can continue to "shoot, move and communicate" even while operating in degraded environments.

Army officials said the experiment demonstrated the counter-PNT system could be successfully launched, operated and recovered in real-world maritime environments.

The testing brought together the U.S. Army, Navy and Space Force, alongside U.S. Space Forces Pacific, Naval Base San Diego and the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, to integrate space, cyber and conventional capabilities during the exercise.

title: Trump floats pulling Blanche's nomination for attorney general to avoid conceding to GOP demands
description: President Donald Trump said Thursday he may pull acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination for the full-time post to avoid conceding to Senate Republicans demanding limits to a sweeping tax au...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday he may pull acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination for the full-time post to avoid conceding to Senate Republicans demanding limits to a sweeping tax audit immunity deal benefiting the president and members of his family that Trump negotiated with his own Department of Justice.

Trump doubled down on choosing his former personal lawyer as the nation's top lawman, calling him "a STAR" and saying he will keep him in the role as acting attorney general until Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina leave office.

"I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd's name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office," Trump posted on his social media site.

Cornyn and Tillis, who both leave office next year, have said they won't back Blanche's nomination without additional assurances in writing about the controversial settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over his leaked tax returns.

In a social media post responding to Trump's suggestion that he may pull Blanche's nomination, Cornyn wrote that the president is "mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis."

"I don't know whether they think they can wait us out or we'll cave, but I assure you we won't," Cornyn told reporters Thursday.

The Senate Judiciary Committee was forced to scrap a planned vote for Thursday to advance Blanche's nomination after the Justice Department and the Republican senators failed to reach a resolution despite hours of negotiations. With all Democratic senators opposed, just one Republican holdout on the committee could sink Blanche's chances for confirmation.

The settlement included the creation of a $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" meant to pay Trump allies who believe they were wronged by the Justice Department that was scrapped after bipartisan outrage about the potential of payouts going to violent Jan. 6 rioters. Officials have said that another piece of the settlement — granting Trump and members of his family immunity from tax audits — remains in place.

Through Blanche has repeatedly insisted that the "Anti-Weaponization fund" is dead, skeptical lawmakers have pushed for a commitment in writing — especially since Trump has expressed continued support for the idea.

A crucial sticking point appeared to be the settlement's audit immunity provision that said the U.S. government is "forever barred and precluded" from scrutinizing or prosecuting Trump, his sons and the Trump organization's current and past tax examinations. Cornyn and Tillis are pressing Trump's administration to modify the agreement to make clear that it covers only existing audits and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings.

Tillis characterized the president's position as "win a battle, lose a war."

"It makes no sense to me," Tillis told reporters Thursday. "This is not popular. The president's not winning on this issue. It is killing some of our candidates because they can't explain it. And now, it looks like they weren't being honest when they said it was inoperative."

While the majority of Republican senators oppose the settlement, the main pushback to Blanche has come from Cornyn, who lost his seat earlier this year when Trump opposed him in a GOP primary. Trump has also frequently targeted Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for re-election and has criticized the administration over the pardons of Jan. 6 rioters and other matters.

Through it would be politically embarrassing for the Trump administration, pulling Blanche's nomination would likely have little practical impact on the management of the Justice Department.

Blanche can still lead the department as either acting attorney general or deputy attorney general, the No. 2 post he was confirmed to last year. The deputy attorney general, who runs the day-to-day operations of the law enforcement agency, is able to perform the duties of the attorney general if that post is vacant.

"I don't know whether they think they can wait us out or we'll cave, but I assure you we won't," Cornyn said Thursday of the Trump administration.

title: ‘Am I paying for the vibes?’ Gen Z says it hates capitalism, but their spending patterns show they just don’t like being ripped off
description: They'll wait in line for TikTok's hype, but they want the receipts from Yelp before they commit.
fullText:
Felipe W., a 20-something Yelp Elite reviewer in Dallas, put it bluntly when describing what he looks for before spending money at a new restaurant.

"In reviews, I want things that you can't quantify so easily from the website or before you walk in. What makes it different than other places? What's their business model like? Am I paying for the vibes?"

How do TikTok and Yelp serve different purposes?

Why does Gen Z trust written reviews over influencers?

How does Gen Z research purchases before spending?

What drives Gen Z's skepticism toward AI recommendations?

It's a question that cuts to the center of a contradiction defining an entire generation's economic behavior. Gen Z has built a reputation as anti-capitalist in spirit — skeptical of corporations, vocal about inequality, allergic to anything that feels like a corporate cash grab. And yet this is also the generation that will wait an hour in a TikTok-viral line for a bagel, a matcha, or a $9 pastry, driven by hashtags like #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt, which has racked up billions of views. New research from Yelp, conducted in partnership with Angus Reid Group, suggests the resolution to that contradiction isn't ideological at all. It's about trust.

New research from Yelp, conducted in partnership with Angus Reid Group, suggests the resolution to that contradiction isn't ideological at all and Gen Z doesn't hate capitalism as much as it says it does. It's about value for money.

Gen Z has a reputation for spontaneous, hype-driven spending, but survey data tells a more complicated story. The research, based on a survey of 1,323 Americans ages 18 to 29 fielded by Angus Reid Group from Feb. 2 to 19, 2026, found that across every category tested, an overwhelming majority of Gen Z researches purchases on at least one platform before buying: 97% for restaurants, 94% for beauty, 93% for fitness and wellness, 92% for home services, and 84% for professional services.

That doesn't mean Gen Z isn't spending. Food remains the top outlet: 78% of respondents said they'd bought takeout or delivery in the past month, and 72% had dined out in person, with both categories up 45% year over year.

When a little extra cash lands in their pocket from a bonus or a gift, 74% said they'd put it toward dining out and 70% toward takeout. The picture isn't a generation retreating from consumption. It's one that consumes constantly while auditing every purchase along the way, a pattern PwC's consumer research has called the "Gen Z paradox" — spending less overall while expecting more from every dollar spent.

That auditing instinct shows up most clearly in how Gen Z weighs sources. The survey found Gen Z trusts detailed written reviews over influencer recommendations by wide margins — 78% to 59% for dining out, and 81% to 61% when picking a service professional like a hairstylist or a contractor. Beyond that, 77% of respondents said they trust platforms with detailed written reviews over those offering only star ratings when researching services, and 76% said the same for restaurants.

title: I went to Cracker Barrel for a late lunch and have some advice for the new CEO on what should change
description: I went to Cracker Barrel and little has changed under the outgoing CEO. Maybe the new boss will freshen up the menu.
fullText:
Cracker Barrel is switching CEOs, the chain said on Monday.

David Deno will take over after Julie Masino spent nearly three years trying to improve results.

I went to a Cracker Barrel location in Virginia to see what the next CEO has to work with.

Cracker Barrel is at a crossroads — again.

The Southern restaurant chain is getting a new CEO, it said on Monday. David Deno will take over as Cracker Barrel's top executive next month, replacing Julie Masino, who has been CEO since late 2023.

In her time as CEO, Masino oversaw changes at Cracker Barrel in an effort to reverse the chain's declining sales and attract more customers to its antique-filled dining rooms. "We're just not as relevant as we once were," she said on an earnings call in 2024.

Last year, Cracker Barrel tried to rebrand with a more modern logo, drawing mixed reactions. It reversed course after public blowback, including from President Donald Trump. The chain also hit pause on restaurant renovations that involved a lighter color scheme and less kitsch adorning its walls.

Since the failed rebrand, Cracker Barrel's quarterly sales continue to decline. And as Masino leaves the CEO role, Cracker Barrel looks a lot like it did when she took over three years ago.

Soon, Deno will need to find a winning strategy for Cracker Barrel, said Wendy Zajack, adjunct professor of marketing at Georgetown's McDonough School of Business.

One chain that's pulled off a turnaround after facing similar troubles is Chili's, Zajack said. The brand is outperforming casual-dining rivals like Applebee's and Red Lobster in sales and traffic growth.

Chili's revamped its menu, keeping some longtime menu items while adding new ones, such as its Triple Dipper, a trio of appetizers that diners can customize. It has also advertised meal deals to inflation-weary diners and gone after Gen Z customers on social media.

"If Cracker Barrel can unlock this formula, it has a fighting chance," she said.
