title: Montana man hikes out of the mountains to get help after he was impaled by a trekking pole
description: David Cifaldi and his two hiking companions were crossing Montana's ominous Froze-to-Death Plateau and approaching the top of the state's highest peak when their adventure took a bizarre and dangerous...
fullText:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — David Cifaldi and his two hiking companions were crossing Montana's ominous Froze-to-Death Plateau and approaching the top of the state's highest peak when their adventure took a bizarre and dangerous turn: Cifaldi slipped and impaled himself on his trekking pole as he fell.

The 44-inch (112-centimeter) steel-tipped pole passed through the flesh beneath Cifaldi's left arm, missing any vital organs, and protruded from his back. After conferring with his friends — and considering the high cost of a helicopter rescue — Cifaldi knew who would save him: himself.

"I was like, 'We've got to get off this mountain.' And they're both like, 'I don't know about that,'" Cifaldi said of his friends' initial reaction. "I'm pretty confident this is outside my chest wall. 'Tis but a flesh wound."

The 32-year-old nurse, who works in wound care at a hospital in Billings, Montana, did a self-assessment. He was alert. There was little pain or blood. And the pole wasn't moving. The group used a satellite-based communication device, a Garmin inReach, to contact local authorities and inform them of their plan to self-rescue.

Then they started hiking out. They carefully descended from the plateau along an unmarked route, navigating through boulders and snowfields before bushwhacking their way to an established trail.

After more than six hours in which they traveled about 10 miles (16 kilometers) and descended roughly 5,000 feet (1,500 meters), the group reached a trailhead where one of them, Cifaldi's friend Jesse Ross, had parked a vehicle.

"The only reason it was possible at all was his confidence," Ross recalled. "Who are we to say anything? He's the medical person. Our job is just to support at that point."

Cifaldi had long wanted to climb Granite Peak. At 12,800 feet (3,900 meters), Montana's tallest mountain is prone to unpredictable weather including dangerous lightning storms and bitter cold. Hundreds of people annually try to reach the rocky summit; many come up short. In 2019, authorities said a 65-year-old Minnesota man who was an experienced climber fell about 150 feet (45 meters) to his death after reaching nearly the top of Granite Peak with his son.

As Cifaldi and his companions started hiking out, the pole awkwardly sticking out of his side, Stillwater County Search and Rescue team commander Ty Williams monitored the group's progress via a dispatcher who took calls from the group.

The first call came in at 9:44 a.m. on July 20, right after Cifaldi impaled himself. At 1:30 p.m. the trio said they were getting closer to the trailhead and to let the nearest hospital know they were coming, Williams said.

"There was no danger to anybody else. He didn't want our help and so we're not going to essentially violate his rights or go against his wishes by forcing our help on him," Williams said.

When they arrived, they were told Cifaldi needed more advanced treatment in Billings. So they got back in Ross' truck and kept driving to the hospital where he works, St. Vincent Regional Hospital.

Doctors removed the pole, bandaged him up and Cifaldi was back at work this week.

"I think 99 times out of a hundred I would make the same decision," Cifaldi said as he sat in Ross' front yard in Billings. "Search and rescue coming to help you is free. The flight's not. That was a factor in me deciding to self-rescue. But the fact that I had two experienced great friends with me and we had the ability to contact search and rescue if something went wrong made that a lot more of an easy decision."

title: Brewery that promised free beer when Trump dies loses alcohol permit
description: A brewery whose owner once offered free beer when President Trump dies is set to lose its alcohol permit but vows to fight the decision.
fullText:
A Wisconsin brewery whose owner once promised to give away free beer if President Donald Trump dies is set to lose its alcohol permit, state officials confirmed to USA TODAY on July 29.

Minocqua Brewing Company, owned by outspoken progressive activist Kirk Bangstad, will have its alcohol permit revoked Aug. 4, according to the state's Department of Revenue.

The action follows a June raid in which state officials seized canned beer from Bangstad's company, alleging it had been transported into Wisconsin from Illinois without the required permits and taxes, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, part of the USA TODAY Network.

"The Wisconsin Division of Alcohol Beverages is dedicated to the fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverages regulations in Wisconsin," the agency said in a statement. "The division is required to follow and implement state law, including ensuring permit holders and licensees follow all applicable laws and regulations."

Bangstad, who describes Minocqua Brewing Company as "the state's most progressive brewery," blasted the state's decision in a newsletter and asked supporters to contribute to a legal defense fund.

"We're going to fight the state of Wisconsin tooth and nail, and once again, they'll have to pry me out of my taprooms before I stop selling beer to thirsty progressives who come to visit us," Bangstad wrote July 26.

He called the revocation "heavy-handed" and said he intends to challenge the decision.

The permit revocation comes about three months after FBI agents interviewed Bangstad over a social media post that appeared to reference an alleged assassination attempt against Trump following the White House Correspondents' Dinner on April 25.

Authorities said Cole Allen tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired a shotgun outside the ballroom where Trump and members of his Cabinet were gathering.

In a Facebook post from the brewery's account, Bangstad wrote: "Well, we almost got #freebeerday. Either a brother or sister in the Resistance needs to work on their marksmanship or he faked another assassination to get a positive news cycle."

Video later posted by Bangstad showed FBI agents questioning him and his attorney about the comment, including whether he or anyone he knew intended to harm Trump or Vice President JD Vance or supported groups with that goal.

Bangstad and his attorney told agents they neither planned nor wished harm on Trump or Vance and did not support any groups advocating violence against them.

Bangstad has frequently made headlines for blending political activism with his brewery business, often using his platforms to criticize Trump and other Republicans. The permit fight is the latest chapter in a dispute with state regulators that has played out in courtrooms, government offices and the public arena for years.

With the Aug. 4 deadline approaching, Bangstad says he plans to challenge the revocation in court as state officials move forward with pulling the brewery's permit.

Contributor: Molly Beck, The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, part of the USA TODAY network

title: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea form 'axis of aggressors' that could overwhelm US, book warns
description: A new report documents 616 instances of security cooperation among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, warning of a dangerous simultaneity problem.
fullText:
China, Russia, Iran and North Korea are acting as a strategically aligned bloc even without a formal mutual-defense treaty, according to a new Foundation for Defense of Democracies book warning that their cooperation could leave the United States confronting multiple crises simultaneously.

The book, "Axis of Aggressors: Countering the Cooperation of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea," examines how the four authoritarian governments support one another across military, economic, cyber and technology domains.

Its authors acknowledge that the grouping is not a NATO-style alliance. It has no unified command, comprehensive defense commitment or complete trust among its members. But they argue that its practical effects are already visible in active conflicts.

Trump To Confront Xi At High-stakes Summit Over China Backing For Iran, Russia

"I just got back from a couple of weeks in Ukraine, and when I'm sitting in Ukraine, it's really obvious to me that Ukraine is fighting Russia, North Korea, Iran and China," retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, one of the book's three authors, told Fox News Digital.

Montgomery pointed to North Korean ammunition and troops, Iranian drones and production expertise, and Chinese economic and technological support for Moscow.

"China is backstopping the whole thing, providing the economic backstop to Russia's economy so they can survive this four-year catastrophic event for Russia," Montgomery said. "They're providing microelectronics that we see in ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles."

The book's researchers documented 616 instances of security cooperation among the four governments from Jan. 1, 2019, through Dec. 31, 2025, including arms transfers, weapons development, military exercises, intelligence sharing and military exchanges.

The central danger, Montgomery said, is what the book calls the "simultaneity problem."

"We don't get to handle these with a singularity anymore. We have to handle this with a simultaneity," he said. "And I don't think we can handle two problems at once, much less three or four."

During a potential confrontation between China and Taiwan, Montgomery said, North Korea could threaten South Korea or conduct limited attacks intended to pin down U.S. forces. A conflict involving Russia and NATO's Baltic members could be accompanied by Iranian terrorism or other hostile activity.

Three Key Reasons Why America Cannot Afford To Lose Taiwan To Communist China

The book identifies China-Russia military cooperation as the axis's most consequential bilateral relationship. Chinese dual-use products have helped sustain Russia's defense industrial base, while Moscow is transferring technology and battlefield lessons that could assist China in a Pacific conflict.

North Korea has supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds, ballistic missiles and troops, while Moscow has assisted Pyongyang's missile, space, drone and nuclear programs, according to the book.

Iran has provided Russia with drones and production knowledge. The book warns that Russian and Chinese assistance could also help Tehran rebuild military capabilities damaged during its conflicts with Israel and the United States.

"The longer they can entangle the United States, whether it was in Ukraine or in Iran, China and Russia are the primary beneficiaries," Montgomery said.

Economic ties underpin the military cooperation, according to co-author Elaine Dezenski, who described the four-country economy as a "fractured alignment."

"These four players are bound together more by necessity than they are by a specific trust or shared strategy among them," Dezenski told Fox News Digital. "China needs energy. Russia and Iran need buyers for their oil and gas. And North Korea needs any lifeline that it can get."

China purchases discounted Russian and Iranian energy while providing goods, technology and access to its domestic market.

The relationships remain unequal. Russia and Iran compete to sell similar products, while China can seek other suppliers. But Dezenski said those divisions should not obscure the benefits the cooperation provides.

"The economics of this very much underpin the foundations for the military engagement that we see," she said.

The book says China purchases as much as 95% of Iran's oil exports. Some sanctioned oil is routed through third countries, relabeled or processed by independent Chinese refineries known as "teapots."

"The export juggernaut that is China today is fueled by sanctioned oil and gas," Dezenski said.

Trump May Claim He Won The Fight With Iran, But There's A Bigger War Already Underway

Dezenski also warned that China, Russia and Iran are developing payment systems outside traditional Western banking infrastructure. More trade is being settled in yuan through China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, potentially reducing Washington's ability to enforce sanctions through the dollar system.

"We need to really think about that sooner rather than later, before this alternative payment system becomes too big to tackle," Dezenski said.

Montgomery said the line between criminal hackers and government operatives is often deliberately blurred in all four countries.

"These regimes routinely outsource work to criminal groups to keep their own hands clean, and those groups are increasingly networking with each other," he said.

The book cites ties involving Iranian cybercriminals and Russian ransomware groups, Chinese actors on Russian dark-web forums, and Russian and North Korean state-backed hackers using shared operational infrastructure.

Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition and a former State Department official during the first Trump administration, said drone warfare demonstrates how assistance moves among the countries.

"Chinese components are used to create Iranian drones, which are then deployed by the Russians against Ukrainian civilians," Filipetti told Fox News Digital.

She said the relationship has also endangered American troops, pointing to the January 2024 Tower 22 attack in Jordan, which killed three U.S. Army Reserve soldiers and wounded more than 40 service members.

"The military and ideological relationship between Russia and Iran is not just a theoretical threat to the United States — American service members have been killed as a result of it," Filipetti said.

Filipetti said the attack used an Iranian drone and Russian tactics developed during the war in Ukraine. "These adversaries don't agree on everything, but they do on one thing: to reorient the world away from America and the West," she said. "Our service members and citizens will continue to suffer until we treat the threat as the united threat it is."

Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton said the danger stems not only from military modernization in each country, but from the degree to which the four governments are increasingly coordinating.

"I couldn't agree more with the underlying findings the authors present regarding the rapid military modernization unfolding across multiple domains — air, sea, land, space and cyber — emanating from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea," Newton told Fox News Digital.

"These nation-states represent extraordinary adversarial challenges for the United States. That's concerning enough," he said. "But a major challenge President Trump is facing in his second administration is the level and degree of integration, synchronization and coordination among these four adversaries, who are more unified today than ever in their collective pursuits to threaten U.S. national security interests."

Newton said the changing character of warfare, demonstrated by more than four years of fighting between Russia and Ukraine and the current U.S.-Iran conflict, has compounded the threat.

"Couple that with the changing nature of warfare we've been witnessing," he said, "and the task to defend our nation is now much more complex and daunting."

Retired Air Force Gen. Philip Breedlove, who served as NATO supreme allied commander and commander of U.S. European Command from 2013 to 2016, argued that Washington's language understates the severity of the confrontation.

"We often say that we are in 'strategic competition' with China and Russia. They are at war with us," Breedlove told Fox News Digital.

Breedlove said China, Russia, Iran and North Korea "are not partners looking for cooperation with the U.S.," but governments seeking to "diminish and defeat" American power.

"The enemy gets a vote," Breedlove said. "Our enemies are voting by their support to Russia and Iran."

He added that assistance from the other countries has become increasingly important to Moscow as it struggles to sustain its war.

"Aid is critical to Russia," Breedlove said. "Russia is failing and becoming ever more dependent on its allies."

The authors recommend stronger coordination with allies, expanded defense production, greater protection of U.S. critical infrastructure and more aggressive sanctions enforcement.

Dezenski called for targeting the full network supporting sanctioned Russian and Iranian oil, including refineries, ports, insurers and financiers, rather than focusing primarily on individual vessels.

"We need to treat this axis as a threat, as a combined threat," Montgomery said, "that will confront us in every one of our crisis areas."

title: The Mediterranean's warming waters are drawing hundreds of invasive species
description: The Mediterranean of our ancestors is no more.  Scientists say climate change, caused mainly by burning oil, coal and gas, is making the Mediterranean Sea hotter, bringing hundreds of new and invasive...
fullText:
ROME (AP) — The Mediterranean of our ancestors is no more.

Scientists say climate change, caused mainly by burning oil, coal and gas, is making the Mediterranean Sea hotter, bringing hundreds of new and invasive fish species that decimate indigenous populations.

As biodiversity diminishes, coastal communities will struggle to make ends meet in the ways they've known for generations.

"The Mediterranean of our grandfathers, of our elders, and of the Greeks, of ancient Greece is lost forever. So many of those changes are irreversible," said Ernesto Azzuro, a marine biologist with the Italian National Research Council's Institute for Marine Biological Resources and Biotechnology.

Scientists have designated the Mediterranean as a climate change "hot spot," with its waters expected to warm by 2 to 6 degrees Celsius (3.6 to 10.8 degrees Fahrenheit) by 2100. Heat waves are likely to become more frequent and more extreme, according to the Mediterranean Experts on Climate and Environmental Change, an independent network of scientists.

Ronan McAdam, an oceanographer with the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change, said a key factor in the warming is that the sea is an enclosed basin and warmth can't dissipate like in the vastness of the oceans.

The warming waters have made an inviting new home for invasive species like the spotted puffer fish, a voracious predator and the "worst invader," Azzuro said.

These species are now heading toward France and Spain after entering the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.

The U.N. food and agriculture body's General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean said such invasive species have been present for decades, but their spread accelerated after the early 2000s, coinciding with rising sea temperatures. For example, the lionfish was first recorded in the eastern Mediterranean in 2012 and has expanded rapidly westward.

"The Mediterranean will be even poorer, even with less species, simply because climate change is really making this part of the Mediterranean, especially the eastern part of the Mediterranean, really unsuitable for native species," Azzuro said.

Cyprus, due to its proximity to the Suez Canal, was first to feel the impact of these invasive fish. Lionfish supplanted indigenous stocks like the red mullet to the dismay of fishers, who have seen local varieties popular with customers greatly diminish.

Then there are rabbitfish that can devour algae from the sea bottom, destroying the habitat for many indigenous species.

"We know what should be done. We should reduce the use of fossil (fuels)," said Piero Genovesi Papik, a zoologist with Italy's Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research. "But that's definitely an urgent matter for the humanity, and we all know the solutions, but of course they require a global and joint vision."

Azzuro said about 1,000 invasive species have been identified in the Mediterranean, with 800 of them firmly established.

The changes are stark. Azzuro said the shallows of the eastern Mediterranean have lost 93% of their mollusk population. Along the Adriatic coast, once abundant with mussels, nearly all have died off because of the sea temperatures that at times have exceeded 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).

From Venice in the north to Bari in the south, "the die-off was spectacular," he said. "Unless we … find population able to survive through these different climates, the future of mussels is not a happy future, at least in the Adriatic Sea."

Azzuro said his institute and its partner a few years ago launched a campaign, "Beware of those four," to raise awareness about the dangers that invasive species pose to human health.

For instance, puffer fish is toxic and potentially lethal if consumed by humans. The lionfish's poisonous spikes can badly hurt anyone who's stung.

Scientists are discussing how coastal communities can cope. One way is to commercialize invasive species that are edible. Another is to pay fishers to catch inedible ones like the puffer fish so they can be incinerated.

Some species, like the lionfish, have "clear economic benefits because it's sold at very high prices, especially in some countries," Azzuro said. But fishers haven't taken advantage of the invasive dusky spinefoot, whose population has grown significantly in Italian waters.

Papik, the zoologist, said that while it's "too late" to reverse the spread of invasive species in the Mediterranean, there are practical ways to mitigate the impact.

First is to prevent their further migration by enforcing an international treaty obliging national authorities to treat ballast waters inside incoming ships that may carry such species.

"This is something that is technically doable and that can reduce the number of ... new alien species by 95 to 99%," he said. Another tactic is treating ship hulls with special paint that thwarts unwanted hitchhikers from latching on.

Papik also said fishing policies are being amended that would allow native species to reclaim some of their number, like growing mollusks that are less susceptible to the alien blue crab.

"In the coming years, I think that the challenge will be to restore, to find new ways to restore the environment," Papik said.

title: Washington mother pulls children from school after Pride lesson shown in music class without notice
description: A Washington mother said a Pride-themed lesson from "Queer Kid Stuff" was shown in music class without parent consent or an option to opt out.
fullText:
A Washington mother says she is withdrawing her children from an elementary school after learning a Pride-themed lesson had been presented during music class without advance notice to parents or an opportunity to opt out, raising questions about district policies governing classroom instruction.

"I assumed I had probably missed an email asking for consent, but there was nothing," Maria Varchetto said in communications with school administrators, which she shared with Fox News Digital on Monday. "No advanced notice, no opportunity to review the lesson, no information letting parents know this topic would be discussed. No option to request that our kids be allowed to opt out and participate in an alternative activity. There was nothing."

Varchetto alleged the lesson was presented to elementary school students, including her daughter, on June 15 at Martha Lake Elementary School in the Edmonds School District as part of a music class and that parents were not informed beforehand.

Trump Admin Targets Woke Schools Accused Of Hiding Students' Gender Transitions From Parents

Varchetto said that a video entitled, "Why is Pride in June," from the YouTube account, "Queer Kid Stuff," which, according to the account, "imagines a kinder and more equal future through highly-accessible education and entertainment for kids ages 3+," was shown to her fourth-grade daughter.

The YouTube channel describes itself as an "LGBTQ+ educational webseries for children ages 3+ hosted by a tie-wearing queer lady, Lindsay, and her non-binary best-stuffed friend, Teddy. Gender Studies 101 meets Mr. Rodgers' Neighborhood!"

Varchetto said the incident prompted her to remove her children from the school.

Virginia School District Sued Over Alleged Policy Of Keeping Students' Gender Transitions Hidden From Parents

"We are 100% removing our kids from this school as I have no trust in the leadership," Varchetto said.

Other materials Varchetto said were included were a list of videos by musicians in the LGBTQ+ community, such as Freddie Mercury of Queen, Lil Nas X and Billy Porter dancing in a ballgown on "Sesame Street."

Varchetto told school officials that her daughter recalled hearing during the lesson that students could identify as gay, lesbian, transgender, asexual, nonbinary or Two-Spirit.

She said an administrator told her she had not been aware those topics were part of the classroom discussion, leaving Varchetto wondering whether the lesson included more than the materials she had been shown.

Trump Administration Opens Four Title Ix Investigations Into Michigan And North Carolina School Districts

"No handouts were sent home (which is typical for music class)," Varchetto told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Varchetto said she asked the school for a copy of the lesson materials but was told they could only be reviewed in person rather than sent electronically. She also said parents were not notified beforehand that the lesson would be taught, were not given an opportunity to opt their children out, and received no advance communication about its content.

She said that cultural lessons were taught every month for the theme of that month, but that Pride month was left off of the list of lessons.

"I feel mad they did this, mad they hid it," Varchetto said. "I feel insulted, offended, angry, and sad that my kids are now being taken out of a lifestyle they've grown to love, away from the friendships they've built, all because this one teacher didn't care to ask permission and a principal lied and hid it."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Edmonds School District said, "The lesson was not part of a districtwide Pride curriculum. It was a music lesson developed by the school's music teacher that highlighted the contributions of influential musicians, including some who identify as LGBTQ+."

The spokesperson continued, "The purpose of the lesson was to teach music and music history through the lives and contributions of notable artists. Discussions about an artist's background or identity were included as relevant biographical context, similar to how students may learn about other aspects of historical figures' lives that helped shape their experiences and contributions."

The spokesperson added, "We expect instructional materials to be age-appropriate and aligned with district expectations and state standards. As with any concern raised about classroom instruction, we will work with the school administrator to determine whether they met those expectations."

title: Bryan Johnson says he might have taken 'this whole longevity thing too far'
description: Longevity zealot Bryan Johnson has expressed some doubts about his quest to live forever.
fullText:
Bryan Johnson says he is having second thoughts about his antiaging experiment.

In an X post, the famous biohacker said he might have taken the "whole longevity thing" too far.

Johnson was diagnosed with an autoimmune disease this year. He also took shrooms twice.

Longevity evangelist Bryan Johnson says he is having second thoughts.

The tech entrepreneur, who has transformed his body into a highly measured experiment in antiaging and longevity, is now expressing some doubts about his famous work.

"Been thinking things over and wonder if I've taken this whole longevity thing too far," Johnson wrote on X on Thursday.

For someone who has so enthusiastically devoted so much time and money to this experiment, it was easy to wonder whether he had been hacked. A day earlier, he said people may live to be 500 years old.

Johnson did not immediately reply to a request for comment from Business Insider.

It's been an eventful year in Johnson's campaign against aging. Earlier this month, he said he had been diagnosed with gastritis — an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the stomach lining — that had gone undetected for years despite his extensive health testing. After the diagnosis, he said he would try to reverse what is considered by doctors to be an incurable condition.

He also took a healthy dose, twice, of psilocybin mushrooms, which, rather famously, can impact how one sees the world. He livestreamed his experience while taking almost 5 grams of the B+ strain of Psilocybe cubensis.

After analyzing the data, Johnson said the mushrooms offer "a compelling case for longevity potential."

"Psilocybin calmed my body and mind," he added.

Since selling the payments company Braintree, Johnson has spent millions a year in a regimented program to reverse aging. He officially launched Project Blueprint in 2021.

His protocol has included an early bedtime, a tightly controlled diet, daily exercise, supplements, prescription drugs, frequent bloodwork, scans, an omnipresent team of doctors, and experimental treatments. He has described himself as perhaps the most biologically measured person in history.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Spain to deploy military to restore order in Ceuta after thousands of people breach Morocco’s border
description: Spain will deploy its military to restore order at its border with Morocco in Ceuta after thousands of migrants streamed into the tiny Spanish territory.  The announcement comes after local authoritie...
fullText:
CEUTA, Spain (AP) — Spain will deploy its military to restore order at its border with Morocco in Ceuta after thousands of migrants streamed into the tiny Spanish territory.

The announcement comes after local authorities in Ceuta had asked the central government in Madrid for reinforcements to manage a border crisis that had been building up before boiling over on Thursday with large crowds of people breeching the border fence.

Spain's government said Thursday evening it would send the Armed Forces to help the Civil Guard "to maintain security in the city of Ceuta." It also announced that Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would join Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska and visit Ceuta Friday.

"The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, who police the border told The Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed."

Achraf Maimouni, a member of the Moroccan Association for Human Rights in northern Morocco, described the situation as ''exceptional.''

"The Tarajal border was opened under unusual circumstances this morning and people crossed,'' he said.

Video footage showed crowds of people, mainly Moroccans, walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach onto local roads. While the majority appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children. Spanish media reported several

"Viva España!" some shouted to a freelance photographer working for the AP. It was not immediately clear what prompted so many migrants to cross to Ceuta.

The escalation at the frontier between Spain and Morocco comes after a surge in migrants attempting to reach the small exclave, mainly by swimming, on Wednesday. At least three people died yesterday attempting to reach Ceuta by sea, Sbihi and activists in both Morocco and Ceuta reported.

Moroccan authorities have not publicly commented on the crossings, and the interior ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Spain's Interior Ministry said the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police are stopping "numerous people" who are trying to cross the border. Both countries agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally."

Spain's interior ministry earlier said it would guarantee the safety of citizens and the integrity of the nation's border but that the government could not declare a national emergency - as local authorities had asked - over migration concerns.

Ceuta authorities had previously linked the spike to a Spanish Supreme Court decision earlier this month that migrants who arrive by sea cannot be immediately pushed back across the border without due process, unlike those who cross into Spain by land — by climbing over the border fence, for example.

But some activists in Morocco expressed doubt that the ruling was behind the surge, arguing most migrants would have been unaware of such legal decisions.

Spain is a main point of arrival into Europe for migrants seeking better economic opportunities or an escape from violence in their home countries.

To reach Ceuta, located on the northern African coast, migrants often swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq, covering about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) to reach Spanish territory. Others attempt the crossing from the nearby town of Belyounech, where the distance is shorter.

The scenes of people streaming across the frontier recall the border crisis of May 2021 when more than 8,000 migrants poured into Ceuta in just two days.

At the time, Morocco was accused of easing border controls and allowing migrants to cross into the Ceuta after Spain allowed Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali to receive treatment at a Spanish hospital, triggering a diplomatic crisis between Rabat and Madrid. The pro-independence Polisario Front for decades has claimed to be the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi people of the Western Sahara, disputed with Morocco.

Juan Jesús Vivas, the head of Ceuta's regional government, called for the national government to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border "to guarantee the inviolability of the frontier and citizen safety."

He had warned Wednesday that migrant reception centers were overwhelmed with hundreds of people sleeping on the streets after more than 1,500 migrants entered the territory in the past week. But thousands more crossed overnight and Thursday.

Spain's Interior Ministry, which tracks irregular migration, would not confirm the number of migrants who had made it to Ceuta in the last few days but said it would publish its next migration report on Aug. 3. As of July 15, nearly 3,000 migrants had entered Ceuta by land or sea this year, according to ministry figures.

Legislation covering a declaration of national emergencies does not consider migration flows as a risk to national security, according to the ministry, which said government administrations are "coordinating to respond with speed and efficacy to the situation in Ceuta."

Ceuta, which is perched on a historical isthmus, has been a Spanish possession since 1580. Its mixed population of Christians and Muslims, Spanish and Moroccan residents and day workers, live in relative harmony behind a border fence that many desperate migrants from across Africa attempt to cross for a better life in Europe.

Brito reported from Barcelona, Spain. AP journalists Joseph Wilson in Barcelona and Akram Oubachir in Casablanca, Morocco, contributed to this report.

title: Father who gave gun to Apalachee High School shooter sentenced to serve 15 years in prison
description: A man who gave his son the gun he used to kill two students and two teachers at Apalachee High School in Georgia was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison.  Colin Gray’s sentencing comes days after...
fullText:
A man who gave his son the gun he used to kill two students and two teachers at Apalachee High School in Georgia was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison.

Colin Gray's sentencing comes days after his son, Colt Gray, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole in the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at the school 45 miles (70 kilometers) northeast of Atlanta. Colt Gray, 16, had pleaded guilty to murder and other charges.

Judge Nicholas Primm, who also sentenced Colt Gray, was blunt in addressing the elder Gray: "It is clear you failed as a parent." But he said punishing crimes of negligence is particularly difficult because there was no intent to commit a crime.

"My heart aches for everyone that was there that day, for all of you that have been impacted by it. But the law requires that I set aside emotion. I don't get to sentence with passion. I have the nearly impossible task of sentencing you without passion despite the immeasurable heartache that you caused," Primm said.

Gray, 55, is one of a handful of American parents who have been criminally charged after their children were accused in shootings.

A jury in March found Colin Gray guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of two 14-year-old students, Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo. Georgia law defines second-degree murder as causing the death of a child by committing the crime of cruelty to children. Gray was also found guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the killings of teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53.

Another teacher and eight other students were wounded, seven of them hit by gunfire.

Family members of those who died and victims of the shooting, many of whom also spoke during Colt Gray's sentencing, condemned what they said were Colin Gray's failures as a parent and urged the judge to give him the maximum sentence.

"This wasn't unavoidable. This was preventable. Because of the choices made inside the Gray household, four families were handed life sentences of grief," said Breanna Schermerhorn, whose son was killed.

"He did not pull the trigger but purchased and left a firearm accessible to a minor," said Shayna Aspinwall, whose husband was killed. She said the sentence must take into account "the families left behind who must carry the grief and trauma for the rest of our lives."

The judge addressed those in the courtroom after announcing the sentence: "This only closes the legal chapter for this horror. The pain, the heartache, they continue. I understand that. I hope all of you know this community loves you, and I ask that God gives you peace."

Prosecutors said Colin Gray gave his son the rifle as a Christmas gift along with ammunition, a gun sight and other shooting accessories.

An investigator testified that Colt Gray carried the semiautomatic rifle onto the school bus with the barrel sticking out and wrapped in poster board. The teenager left his second-period class and went to a bathroom, emerged with the rifle and shot people in the hallway and a classroom, the investigator said.

Colt Gray, who was 14 at the time of the shooting, had shown signs of deteriorating mental health in the weeks leading up to the killings, according to testimony. He belonged to a "true crime community" online where he and other young people discussed their obsession with mass shooters, an investigator testified.

The teen's mother, Marcee Gray, who was separated from Colin Gray, told investigators she had argued with her estranged husband weeks before the shooting, asking him to secure his guns and restrict their son's access.

Defense attorney Brian Hobbs asked the judge for a sentence of 10 years in prison followed by 10 years on probation. Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith said Gray deserved a sentence of 80 years in prison.

Hobbs argued that Colt Gray "actively hid the depth of his involvement" in the online community obsessed with mass shooters, and the red flags enumerated by prosecutors were outliers among happier moments.

Smith countered that Colin Gray ignored "a substantial and unjustifiable risk."

"This was the risk that he was ignoring, that there would be a mass shooting of children at a school, and he gave his son the exact tool he would need to accomplish this," Smith said.

Prosecutors have in recent years held parents responsible when they believe they can prove a parent contributed to a killing.

Jennifer and James Crumbley were the first U.S. parents to face such charges after their son, Ethan, killed four students and wounded others at Michigan's Oxford High School in 2021. Like Colin Gray, they were unaware of their son's plans but had gifted him a gun before the shooting. They are serving 10-year prison terms for involuntary manslaughter. Hobbs, the defense attorney, urged the judge to use that sentence as a guide.

The judge called these cases "divisive." There would have been no crime by the father if the son hadn't brought a gun to school and shot people, he noted. But he said Colin Gray could have locked up the guns, kept ammunition out of the house, had someone else keep the guns and gotten his son counseling.

"You were convicted because the warning lights were flashing brighter and brighter and you didn't get him help and you didn't remove his access to the guns," Primm said.

This story has been corrected to show the school is called Apalachee High School, not Appalachee.

title: Obama endorses Iowa Democrat Josh Turek for Senate
description: Former President Obama on Wednesday endorsed Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Iowa. In a roughly two-minute video Turek’s campaign shared on YouTube, the state representative takes on ...
fullText:
Former President Obama on Wednesday endorsed Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Iowa.

In a roughly two-minute video Turek's campaign shared on YouTube, the state representative takes on Obama in a game of IOWA — a variation of the basketball shoot-around game HORSE.

Turek, who was born with spina bifida and has used a wheelchair since childhood, won two gold medals playing for the U.S. men's national wheelchair basketball team in the Paralympics. Obama is a diehard basketball fan who roots for the Chicago Bulls and reveals his March Madness picks each year.

During their game, the two discussed their Mount Rushmore of the greatest NBA players ever — with Obama putting Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Magic Johnson on his list, and Turek including Jordan, James, Abdul-Jabbar and Bill Russell.

They also discussed Obama's victory in the 2008 Iowa Democratic caucus, which fueled his run to the nomination and later the presidency.

"Of all the things I've done in politics, Iowa was my favorite thing," Obama told Turek. "There was just a magic about regular folks showing up, in gyms like this and just talking out, 'How do we move our state forward, how do we move the country forward?'"

This marks the second Senate race Obama has publicly weighed in on, after he campaigned in May alongside Texas state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the Lone Star State.

Turek, a member of the Iowa House since 2023, is taking on Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) in the race to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa).

If Turek wins in November, he would be the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Hawkeye State since former Sen. Tom Harkin won his final race in 2008. A Democratic presidential nominee also has not won Iowa since Obama did in 2012.

But Democrats have expressed optimism about Turek's chances of defeating Hinson in November. He represents a district that President Trump carried three times and has reached out to voters across the ideological spectrum.

A survey conducted by Fox News last month found Turek leading Hinson by 4 points, outside the poll's margin of error.

In his ad alongside Obama, Turek said voters in Iowa "are feeling that hope, that optimism, for the first time in a long time" — a sentiment the former president agreed with.

"Not only did I get whooped," Obama said, after losing his game of IOWA to Turek. "But you've got here a man of character, somebody who knows how to win."

"Now, the ball's in your court, Iowa. Let's make sure that we send Josh Turek to the United States Senate," he added.

fullText:
DETROIT, July 30 (Reuters) - Ford CEO Jim Farley told employees in a town hall on Thursday that the company is preparing for the possibility that Chinese automakers could enter the American market in the ‌next five to 10 years, even though the country has erected numerous trade barriers to cars from China, ‌according to three people who viewed the meeting.

What trade barriers currently block Chinese cars?

Why are Chinese automakers gaining global market share?

How is Ford preparing for Chinese automotive competition?

When could Chinese automakers enter the US market?

Farley has been among the most vocal about how competitive Chinese auto giants like BYD are in the industry. ​Ford is preparing to roll out a family of affordable electric vehicles that it engineered from the ground up to match the cost and efficiency of the Chinese companies.

The Ford chief, along with other senior leaders, said in a question-and-answer portion of the town hall that it is more likely Chinese companies would enter the market at the latter end of that range. The comments come as the ‌U.S. Senate is pushing to expand a ⁠ban on Chinese car sales in the world's second-largest and most lucrative auto market.

A Ford spokesperson declined to comment on discussions that took place during a private meeting with employees.

Leaders at the Dearborn, ⁠Michigan, automaker have previously warned that China was on America's doorstep, but have not been as specific with the time frame as executives were in the Thursday meeting.

Ford Executive Chair Bill Ford spoke on the topic earlier this month.

"We have to go toe-to-toe with China," Ford ​said at ​an Axios event. "We can't expect to keep them out forever, and ​we have to be able to beat them at ‌their own game."

Chinese automakers have gained significant market share in neighboring Mexico, and under a trade deal with Canada are allowed to sell a limited number of EVs there. Auto industry experts see Canada, which is very similar to its U.S. neighbor, as a test market for Chinese automakers that are eager to sell to American consumers.

American consumers have signaled increasing interest in these models, surveys show, especially as affordable electric options are scant.

The U.S. currently blocks Chinese electric vehicles through tariffs of about 100%, in addition ‌to U.S. Commerce Department rules banning Chinese software by model year 2027 ​and hardware by model year 2030.

The connected-vehicle rules were adopted in January 2025 ​under U.S. President Joe Biden, based on national security ​concerns around data privacy, and have been kept in place under the Trump administration. Automakers, including ‌Ford, have worked to obtain authorizations under the rule ​to continue selling some China-produced vehicles ​in the United States.

title: Trump retaliates after Iran attack as expert warns regime is growing more dangerous
description: Trump vowed to hit Iran hard after CENTCOM confirmed all ballistic missiles targeting U.S. forces in Jordan were intercepted with no casualties reported.
fullText:
The United States resumed airstrikes inside Iran Wednesday night in retaliation for Tehran's attempted surprise ballistic-missile attack on American forces, as an Iran expert warned that the regime has become increasingly willing to test Washington despite its weakened military capabilities.

"The strikes are a powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attack on U.S. forces based in the Middle East," U.S. Central Command said as the new operation began, according to The Associated Press.

The renewed strikes marked the first U.S. attacks inside Iran since President Donald Trump paused the bombing campaign Friday after 13 consecutive nights to allow diplomacy another chance. Iran's missile launch shattered that brief pause and returned the conflict to direct exchanges between Washington and Tehran.

Trump had signaled the retaliation earlier Wednesday, saying the United States would hit Iran "very hard."

Army Ids 2 Victims Killed In Jordan Air Base Attack; Trump: Iran Will Pay 'Many Times Over'

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the surprise nature of Iran's attack reflected a significant shift in Tehran's strategy.

"What makes this attack different is that it's basically a surprise attack," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. "This is the Islamic Republic matching its deeds with its words," he said. "That means a more risk-tolerant, more confident, perhaps less capable, but more dangerous Iran in the Middle East."

U.S. Central Command said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran at U.S. forces in the region at approximately 5:45 p.m. Eastern Time Tuesday. All were intercepted, and no casualties or damage were immediately reported.

Trump later vowed a forceful response, telling Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that the United States would be "hitting them hard" and that Iran was "going to get a beating." "We're going to beat the f---ing s--- out of them," Trump said.

Us Claws Back Key Concession To Iran After Fresh Attacks On Commercial Ships In Strait Of Hormuz

But Ben Taleblu warned that successful interceptions alone may not restore deterrence. He argued that Tehran has repeatedly learned that it can fire on American forces, absorb a U.S. response and then attempt to dictate when the exchange ends.

"The dangerous lesson for America here is that you have to treat every single Iranian missile attack, whether it was successful or not, as being successful," he said. "You can't over-rely on technology because, ultimately, this is not a technological problem. This is a political problem."

The attack came as the nearly five-month conflict threatened to widen across the region.

Iran said it also targeted commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, while the United States and Saudi Arabia jointly struck Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq following drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The operation marked the first time Riyadh publicly acknowledged participating in strikes alongside Washington, potentially opening a new front in the confrontation, Reuters reported.

Two Us Service Members Killed In Iranian Strikes On Jordan, Centcom Says

The renewed fighting also threatens already-fragile negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran rejected an Omani proposal for joint regional management of the waterway, insisting on broader control over shipping routes through the strait.

The attack followed a far deadlier Iranian attack on U.S. forces in Jordan earlier in July. That strike hit housing used by American troops at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, killing two U.S. service members and wounding several others.

The United States subsequently struck Iranian targets, but Ben Taleblu argued that Tehran continues to believe it can absorb retaliation, fire back and dictate when each cycle of fighting ends.

He said the United States must respond while preparing for another Iranian counterattack, warning that allowing Tehran to claim it had "closed the round" after retaliating would reinforce the regime's belief that it can dictate the pace of the conflict.

"The U.S. certainly does need to respond, and President Trump indeed has promised to respond with some very colorful language, but it has to be prepared for the Iranian response," he said.

Original article

title: I Upgraded to an Otterbox, and It Saved My Brand New iPhone's Screen
description: It's worth protecting your $1,000 device with a $60 case.
fullText:
Over the years, I have cracked more phone screens than I'd like to admit. It usually starts as a small crack in the corner, only to eventually spread across the screen like a spiderweb. That's actually how I ended up needing to upgrade to a new iPhone (the 17 Pro) last month. Only this time, I swore I was going to protect it properly.

In the past, I'd avoided bulky cases for silly style reasons. But sleek phones are also, as I have proven again and again, fragile phones. So this time, I went all in: an Otterbox case, a screen protector, and a MagSafe wallet. If I was going to upgrade my phone, I figured I might as well upgrade my whole relationship with it.

I put my Otterbox case and screen protector to the test with truly comedic timing. Within hours of securing my new phone in the Otterbox protections, it fell out of my pocket while I was biking. I am who I am.

I picked the phone up braced for the worst—which was justified, since the screen protector was, in fact, cracked. The actual iPhone screen underneath, however, was completely fine. This is because the screen protector did exactly what it's designed to do: It takes the hit so your $1,000 phone doesn't have to.

I peeled off the screen protector and ordered a replacement for $40. Meanwhile, my actual phone, underneath the Otterbox and now a fresh protector, thankfully remains undamaged.

The MagSafe wallet has turned out to be an upgrade in its own right, too. Now my cards are attached to the thing I am, for better or worse, incapable of losing track of: my phone.

I'll admit there's an irony in taking this long to arrive at the obvious conclusion that protecting your $1,000 device with a $60 case (and $40 screen protector) is a good trade. Now, when I picture my next phone drop—and there certainly will be one—I'm hopeful that worst case, I'm out another screen protector and five minutes of my day. For someone with my track record of cracking phone screens, an Otterbox case (and accessories) are a no-brainer upgrade.

title: If You Loved ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If the meta and hilarious spinoff to "The Big Bang Theory" is your cup of tea, you will love "Everything Everywhere All at Once."
fullText:
Stuart Fails to Save the Universe might be the most surprising series on TV right now. Another spinoff from the wildly successful The Big Bang Theory, the show’s focus on bit players from the original series and an enthusiastic embrace of its gonzo multiverse plot shaped a fun, fast-paced, and inventive sitcom that both scratches the nostalgic itch for more of that universe and offers something completely fresh and new in it. If you’re looking for more sci-fi hijinx and humor that embraces the multiverse with wit, imagination, and a robust supply of heart (and you’ve already burned through the shows that offer a similar vibe), then there’s precisely one movie you should watch immediately: Everything Everywhere All at Once.

Written and directed by Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (aka the Daniels), Everything Everywhere All at Once is the story of Evelyn Quan Wang (Michelle Yeoh), an unhappy, middle-aged immigrant from China who runs a failing laundromat and is struggling in every aspect of her life, from her relationships with her father (James Hong), husband (Ke Huy Quan), and daughter (Stephanie Hsu) to her upcoming audit with the IRS. At her IRS interview, her body is suddenly controlled and she finds herself face to face with an alternate version of her husband, Waymond, who informs her that there are multiple universes and versions of her, and that she must access the skills and life experience of those alternate versions in order to save the multiverse from destruction by Jobu Tupaki—an alternate version of her daughter, Joy.

If you love the wild ride that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe offers as the gang regularly slides into a new alternate world, Everything Everywhere All at Once is the perfect match. As Evelyn struggles to comprehend the nature of her existence in a multiverse and figure out how to survive the bizarre and mind-blowing attacks Jobu Tupaki sends her way, we are treated to a dizzying range of insane universes. We see Evelyn as a martial arts movie star (not unlike Yeoh in real life), a scientist, a teppanyaki chef, a woman with hot dogs for fingers (in a universe where everyone has hot dogs for fingers) and, in one of the most moving moments, as a literal rock.

If you’re digging the emotional core of the show as Stuart seeks a universe where he is worthy and hasn’t ruined everything, the core premise of Everything will hit you right in the feels. Evelyn has been chosen because she’s the worst version of herself—the version that has consistently failed in everything she’s tried, and thus the version with the most stored potential. Her emotional journey from nihilism and anger to love and acceptance as she learns to fight for what she loves is powerfully moving. Like the show, the movie leverages the character-building aspects of a multiverse, letting us see how a normal, regular person with normal, regular problems might face a terrifyingly abnormal challenge.

Plus, the movie is just fun. How can you watch a scene where mild-mannered Waymond Wang defeats a gang of security guards using multiverse-downloaded fannypack skills and not want to watch the rest of the movie?

Stream Everything Everywhere All at Once on Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

The multiverse may be infinite, but movies about them aren’t. If you’ve watched Everything Everywhere All at Once and need more fun sci-fi stories, here are a few more movies that catch that Stuart vibe.

Douglas Adams’ classic story of an ordinary guy named Arthur Dent who is rescued by his friend (and secret alien) Ford Prefect when Earth is destroyed to make way for a hyperspace bypass isn’t a multiverse story per se, but it has similar elements. That’s thanks to the Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows for faster-than-light travel by passing through every point in every possible universe simultaneously, resulting in some really, really weird stuff (the hilariously inconsistent timeline resulting from the many variations of the story also contributes a sense of multiversity craziness). It’s an absurdist’s dream, riffing on every conceivable sci-fi trope and delivering a surprisingly sweet story of a man struggling with his sense of unimportance in an increasingly confusing existence.

Rent The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy on Prime Video.

You want a bit more edge to your multiverse humor? Check out Deadpool & Wolverine, in which everyone’s favorite merc with a mouth (Ryan Reynolds) has to skip through various universes to find a replacement Wolverine (Hugh Jackman), who famously and nobly died at the end of Logan in 2017, for, er, reasons. It’s absolutely riddled with hilarious bits, fourth-wall breaks, and hyperviolence—but there’s a gooey emotional core to it, as well.

Stream Deadpool & Wolverine on Disney Plus, or rent it on Prime Video.

If Everything Everywhere All at Once is a bit too staid and sedate for your tastes, check out this 1984 fever dream of a sci-fi movie. When rock star, scientist, and surgeon Buckaroo Banzai (Peter Weller) tests a device that allows him to pass through matter, he briefly engages with the 8th dimension—and unwittingly attracts the attention of aliens who wish to use his technology to free their brethren trapped there, putting the existence of humanity at risk. It’s one of the weirdest vibes ever captured on film, but it’s also hilarious and one of the most unique films you’ll ever watch.

Stream The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension on The Roku Channel, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the unexpected twists that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe serves up as he and his friends travel through alternate universes, strap in for John Dies at the End. To say the story is complex would an understatement—it slides between the past, present, and future of various dimensions at a rapid clip—but it kicks off when a man named David (Chase Williamson) is contacted by his recently dead friend, Rob, who tells him about a drug called Soy Sauce that lets folks remember the future and allows entities to creep from one universe into another—and they’re infiltrating David’s universe. It’s wild and often really funny, so if it’s extra you’re looking for, look no further.

Stream John Dies at the End on The Roku Channel, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want to lean a bit more into plain old funny stuff, this modern classic is perfect. There’s no multiverse here, but there is a lot of affectionate humor aimed squarely at sci-fi tropes (especially the Star Trek universe and its, er, passionate fans). Galaxy Quest was a Trek-like TV series that aliens called Thermians believe was a documentary. When their civilization is threatened by a villain named Sarris, they kidnap the cast (including Tim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver, and Sam Rockwell) of the TV series to help them defeat Sarris, and, yes, hilarity ensues. But also a lot of heart and character development, if that’s your bag.

Stream Galaxy Quest on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

title: The Pixel 11's Biggest New Feature Might Be Its Inflated Price Tag
description: The Pixel 11 series will have small upgrades, but a bigger price tag than the Pixel 10.
fullText:
Smartphone manufacturers rarely innovate these days, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. It's a sign that iPhones and Androids have gotten so good, there's little room left for major advancements and upgrades. When a company like Google announces a new smartphone line, most of us aren't expecting something that will convince us to upgrade from its previous generation; rather, you know that if it's time to buy a new phone, the latest generation will likely be the de facto "best" phone you can buy.

So it seems is the case for Google's upcoming Pixel 11 lineup. Rumors suggest that the company is making small updates in some key areas as you might expect, without changing too much from the Pixel 10. The biggest change, it seems, might just be the phone's price tag. If you're considering upgrading to a new Pixel 11 device, know you might just be paying more for it than ever.

As highlighted by Engadget, the overall design of the Pixel 11 line is virtually identical to the Pixel 10. That goes for all rumored models, including the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. If you have a corresponding Pixel 10 device, the Pixel 11 upgrade will have the same screen sizes, which means the lineup will have the following displays:

Pixel 11: 6.3-inches (1080 x 2424)

Pixel 11 Pro: 6.3-inches (1280 x 2856)

Pixel 11 Pro XL: 6.8-inches (1344 x 2992)

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 6.3-inch outer display (1080 x 2342) and 8-inch inner display (2076 x 2160)

The camera bumps will remain unchanged as well, though the hardware itself may get a bit of an upgrade. The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold may ship with 50 MP main cameras, which is a slight bump up from the 48 MP camera on the Pixel 10. The cameras on the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL may get new sensors as well.

While it might seem like you wouldn't be able to tell the difference between the Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 by sight alone, you actually will. That's because the rumors suggest Google will introduce new colors for the lineup. The Pixel 11 may ship in Midnight, Fuchsia, and Moss, while the Pixel 11 Pro may come in Dune, Pine, and Sterling. Finally, the Pixel 11 Pro may ship in Midnight or Pine.

Perhaps the biggest upgrade this year will be the Tensor G6 chip. Engadget says that Google's latest SoC (System-on-a-Chip) is built on a 2nm process, which may be the same as Apple's upcoming iPhone 18 series. While we'll need access to the phone for actual benchmarking and real-world tests, the new chip could offer better battery life and power efficiency than the current Tensor G5.

However, new chips are expected with new smartphone generations. Perhaps the biggest shock this year will be how much you actually have to pay to acquire Google's newest phones. Like Apple, Google may drop the 128GB base model options for the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro, and may instead choose to start at 256GB. While that's good for users who often run out of storage, it takes away the previous base model price tag of $799. Now, the new entry price will be $899: technically the same price, but it will cost $100 more to get a new Pixel than it used to.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, however, may just get a price increase for no other reason than the ongoing memory crisis. Because of sharp demand for RAM and other computer components across the globe, companies are raising prices across the board. As such, Engadget suggests that the Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold may get a €100 increase, which could reflect a $100 increase in the U.S. as well.

If you need the latest and greatest from Google for your next phone, you'll have no choice but to spend the extra money. However, you might be better off finding a good deal on a Pixel 10 or a Pixel 10a. After all, there's not that much difference between the Pixel 11 series to necessarily justify the rumored price increase.

title: Google Docs Is Rolling Out These Three New Gemini Features
description: If you pay for Google's AI features, you can try this new Gemini integration in Google Docs.
fullText:
Google makes both Gemini and Docs, so it's not surprising that you'll find plenty of the former's features while using the latter. Gemini has a ton of Google Docs integration, including reading your text out loud, searching and summarizing your Docs in Drive, and a "Gemini bar" embedded into the app for prompting anytime. It's to the point that it's tough to avoid, which isn't great news for Google Docs users uninterested in AI features.

Of course, that won't stop Google. The company continues to add new Gemini features at a steady clip, and this week is no exception. As Android Authority notes, Gemini is now rolling out new image creation and editing abilities available directly in Google Docs. Google announced the changes in a Workspace update on Tuesday, highlighting how Docs users can tap into Gemini to create and edit images, diagrams, and infographics in their documents.

According to Google, Gemini has three new functions Workspace users can take advantage of. First, users can create infographics or diagrams that summarize the doc in question. You could ask Gemini to do something like "add a diagram that explains the proposal at the top of this doc," or "create an infographic that summarizes the doc visually." Google says Gemini will pull from the context of the doc for these graphics, so these images should reflect what you have written in your doc—excluding the odd hallucination, of course.

In addition, Gemini can "refine existing visuals." You can ask Gemini to adjust the images in your doc with requests like, "change the aspect ratio of this image to 4:3," or "match the image's style to the other images in this doc." Finally, you can also ask Gemini to generate or edit multiple images at once. You could request the AI to create infographics in each section of your doc, or update all images at once.

These new additions to Google Docs aren't rolling out to everyone. Instead, they're exclusive to Workspace users, which includes Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. If you pay for Google's AI features, you can try these out once they roll out on your end. If your school, work, or organization uses Workspace, the same applies. Here's the full list:

Business: Business Standard and Plus

Enterprise: Enterprise Standard, and Plus

Consumer: Google AI Pro and Ultra

Education Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education; Teaching and Learning

title: Pressley signs new Dundee deal but warns of pain ahead
description: Steven Pressley says signing a new contract with Dundee was the "right decision", despite "a lot of pain ahead" for the club.
fullText:
Head coach Steven Pressley says signing a new contract with Dundee was the "right decision", despite "a lot of pain ahead" for the club.

The Dens Park outfit have not disclosed details of Pressley's new deal, but it is believed he remains on a one-year rolling contract.

The 52-year-old replaced Tony Docherty in June 2025 and guided Dundee to an eighth-place finish in the Scottish Premiership last season.

"We'd been discussing [a new contract] for some time," Pressley said. "And obviously I'm delighted to get that over the line.

"From just a personal perspective, it was really important. I've been living up here without my family and my wife for the best part of a year and I think sometimes people forget that managers are actually human beings."

Off the back of the new deal, Pressley's wife is now moving back up to Scotland and he says it was challenging living on his own.

"We're vulnerable," he said. "We have feelings like everybody else and the journey in life of a manager can be very difficult and very lonely at times.

"When you're quite isolated and away from the most important people in your life, it can be challenging."

What is the magic number to win Scottish Premiership?

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Stoke sign defender Graham from Dundee

Aside from the personal benefits, Pressley says Dundee suits him professionally and believes the club are moving in a positive direction, even though he has had to deal with several players leaving this summer.

Defenders Luke Graham and Billy Koumetio have moved to Stoke City and Charlton Athletic, respectively. Goalkeeper Jon McCracken left for Bradford City, while key loanees such as Yan Dhanda, Cameron Congreve and Tony Yogane have returned to their parent clubs.

"I'm very honest about situations," Pressley said. "I think there's still a lot of pain ahead for us. We've lost so many key, influential players from last year. To replace them is very difficult.

"We've brought in players that we have confidence in, but it'll take time to settle. That is one thing I can assure people, that it's going to take time. It did with players last season and it's going to take the same again this year.

"There has to be a degree of patience and understanding."

Pressley admits the backing of managing director John Nelms was key to him extending his stay, and says Motherwell's recent success can provide a blueprint for Dundee.

"I think there's a lot of scope for growth here," he said

"It's difficult to put a timescale on, but I think we've already got a club in Scotland that are a great example to others.

"Motherwell are commanding astronomical transfer fees for players. They're developing their club within. They've qualified for Europe. So that has to be an aspiration of ourselves."

Dundee open their Premiership season with a trip to champions Celtic on Monday night, an "enormous challenge" that Pressley is embracing.

"Celtic haven't lost an opening-day fixture at home for nearly 76 years," he said.

"But I also like those challenges. I think our players respond well to those challenges."

title: Scottish Premiership is back on Friday - here's why you shouldn't miss it
description: BBC Scotland takes a look at the top talking points going into the new Scottish Premiership season.
fullText:
It seems like it was only yesterday traffic cones across Boston were being turned into street art and Billy Gilmour had transformed into a Major League Baseball pitcher.

The star-spangled pizazz has only just subsided after the crashing wave of World Cup disappointment for Scotland, but now we're back to the real stuff.

The Scottish Premiership, surely the globe's top league for compulsive viewing, returns this Friday.

Here's the top takes to hook you back in.

What is the magic number to win Scottish Premiership?

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Hearts' players were on the brink of history and immortality. It was nine minutes away.

Four decades of Old Firm dominance was that close to toppling. The season-long league leaders were drawing with holders Celtic in Glasgow as the game crept into the 87th minute.

It looked like they were just about to hold until Daizen Maeda struck to trigger bedlam in Paradise.

Ugly scenes followed Celtic's third deep into injury time as Hearts headed straight for the team bus, eventually reemerging outside Tynecastle with tears spilling from their faces.

Since then, the backbone of that team has been deconstructed. Boss Derek McInnes has departed for Tynecastle, taking with him captain and talisman Lawrence Shankland, as well as midfield controller Cammy Devlin.

Wouter Vrancken has arrived from Sint-Truiden and the Belgian has suffered a tumultuous start.

A 6-0 hiding from Sturm Graz sent Hearts tumbling out of Champions League qualifying, with the Tynecastle support looking at the club's analytical approach to signings to somehow hoist them back to the lofty heights they hit last term.

"Hearts just look as if it's just a new squad flung in together, with the manager too, trying to find their way," said former striker Ryan Stevenson.

"You don't get time in football, it's game after game after game.

"If you don't get results, we all know what Tynecastle is like. It can be electric, but can they deal with the stadium turning? Are they big enough characters to deal with that?

"If they don't play well, I would give it to mid-September, and it would not be nice."

Are there already worrying signs for Vrancken's Hearts?

The short answer is... well... we don't really know yet.

Last season's domestic double was followed by Martin O'Neill remaining as boss, offering some continuity after the most unique of campaigns.

However, there still has been plenty of disquiet among supporters.

Anti-board sentiment was present last term before and after Brendan Rodgers' shock departure, with Wilfried Nancy's alarmingly short tenure doing little to help.

In a bid to quell matters, a fan engagement programme, external was launched on Thursday.

At the heart of the unrest though, ultimately, is what - and who - happens on the park.

The Parkhead side have made two signings this summer - Camilo Duran and Kasper Hogh - for reported combined fees of around £15m.

However, talismanic forward Daizen Maeda has left to join Ipswich Town and O'Neill is keen to get high-calibre players through the door sooner rather than later.

Celtic have been linked extensively with Real Oviedo and Egypt winger Haissem Hassan, as well as Paderborn midfielder Mika Baur.

"I think we're trying to get some quality into the football club," O'Neill told Sky Sports.

Celtic 'a really good match' for record signing Hogh

The former Ibrox player was so close to legendary status and a league winner's medal with Hearts in May. Now, he's aiming to do just that in Glasgow.

A 2-1 win over St Etienne and a goalless draw with West Ham in pre-season friendlies have offered tentative encouragement. Ultimately, Rangers need consistency and an identity that was lacking last term.

Danny Rohl hauled Rangers in the title hunt going into the split, only to then lose four of their five remaining matches.

Long-term captain James Tavernier has left, so too have goalkeeper Jack Butland and forward Oliver Antman.

McInnes and Rangers appear to have made some shrewd moves in the transfer market already in the opposite direction.

South Africa defender Olwethu Makhanya is the eighth new recruit to arrive, while Shankland has been appointed skipper and the acquisition of young Serbia international midfielder Vanja Dragojevic looks a savvy one.

But is it enough to shift the balance of power away from Glasgow's east end?

Is McInnes era giving Rangers fans fewer fears of failure?

Scotland is not alone with an obsession over video assistant referees and the application of the technology across the game.

Earlier this week associations were told VAR should only intervene over "blatant" incidents.

Incredibly, this will be the fifth season of VAR's use in Scotland and fans still remain divided.

In the most high-profile incident, former Motherwell midfielder Elliot Watt and McInnes were both sanctioned for fuming over the decision to award Celtic a late penalty at Fir Park in the penultimate game of last season.

Watt described it as "the worst VAR decision in history", while McInnes claimed it was "disgusting".

Last week St Johnstone manager Simo Valakari said he believes the system will get better after a meeting with the Scottish Football Association's VAR manager Martin Atkinson.

The Finn also said maybe in Scotland there needs to be more "patience".

As if all that wasn't enough...

We have five managers starting permanent tenures at clubs in McInnes, Vrancken, Alfred Johansson at Motherwell and O'Neill and Craig McLeish taking on the role proper at Celtic and St Mirren respectively.

Speaking of Motherwell, Scotland's answer to Barcelona last season have lost key players in Watt and New Zealand World Cup hero Elijah Just, but have managed to retain their methodical footballing approach as well as the likes of Tawanda Maswanhise and Lukas Fadinger.

Can Johansson kick on from the Jens Berthel Askou blueprint and keep the crowds swelling at Fir Park?

You also have a first full season at Pittodrie for Stephen Robinson and proper grass at Kilmarnock, who have ditched their artificial surface.

As always, the BBC has you covered.

Online, you can 

We will also provide live text coverage of every single Scottish Premiership match.

You can follow the latest video content across all our social channels, as well as on the BBC Scottish Football YouTube channel for bespoke video.

On television, Sportscene has you covered for highlights starting on Friday as Dundee United host Rangers. You can catch the show on BBC iPlayer and BBC One Scotland at 23:35 BST.

And on radio, follow exclusive radio commentary and top punditry on Sportsound, while Stuart Cosgrove and Tam Cowan, the Odd Couple of Scottish Football, will continue to bring you the best petty and ill-informed show on the airwaves, Off The Ball.

title: Wales sprint team trio win Commonwealth gold
description: Wales have won Commonwealth Games gold in the women's team sprint at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome by beating England in the final.
fullText:
Wales have won Commonwealth Games gold in the women's team sprint at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome by beating England in the final.

The Welsh trio of Emma Finucane, Rhian Edmunds and Lowri Thomas defeated Katy Marchant, Sophia Capewell and Rhianna Parris-Smith in a new Commonwealth Games record time of 46.760s.

Wales had set the fastest time in qualifying to set up the gold medal race and delivered the ultimate upgrade on the bronze medal the same trio won in Birmingham in 2022.

It was the 18th medal for Team Wales with three gold, six silver and nine bronze.

This was the third medal for Wales on the opening night of track cycling after silver for Para-cyclist James Ball and his guide Matt Rotherham and bronze for the women's team pursuit.

Unfortunately the men's trio of Lewis Oliva, Steffan Lloyd and Ioan Hepburn could not compete in the team sprint event bronze medal race.

Hepburn made the start line but pulled out after having medical advice.

Trinidad and Tobago were awarded the bronze medal.

title: Raids across UK in crackdown on nuisance car finance texts
description:
